screen.reason: This is YbAu2In (YbInAu2), the Yb member of the cubic Heusler REInAu2 series. The series papers by Besnus et al. (1985 Physica B; 1986 J. Less-Common Met.) describe YbInAu2 as an intermediate-valence compound and report no superconductivity in their abstracts. Later work (neutron paramagnetic scattering, 1995; pressure studies, 1999 and 2022) treats it as an intermediate-valence Kondo system, and none of it mentions superconductivity. Searches for YbAu2In turned up only the different phases YbAu2In4 and Yb2Au3In5. No source reports this composition as a superconductor.
screen.best_lead_title: Structural and magnetic properties of the ternary rare earth (RE) compound series REInAu2 (RE = La to Lu, Y)

screen.reason: This is body-centred tetragonal Ho(Rh1-xRux)4B4 with x = 0.400/0.444 = 0.90, at the Ru-rich end of a well-studied series. Knauf et al. (PRB 29, 2477, 1984) mapped the phase diagram for 0.07 <= x <= 1 above 1.3 K and report an abrupt drop of Tc near x_cr of about 0.40. Knauf et al. (Physica B 1985) extended the bct R(Rh1-xRux)4B4 measurements down to 4 mK and report the same drop for x >= x_cr. Iwasaki et al. (Physica B 148, 1987) state that on the Ru-rich side the magnetic order is ferromagnetic and superconductivity disappears, and Adrian et al. (1987) report a change of magnetic structure near x of about 0.80. The table's superconducting rows all have x <= 0.4, so everything I found agrees that x = 0.90 is not superconducting. This is from abstracts only; the figures in Thomae et al. (JLTP 1986) would give the exact lower temperature limit for x = 0.90.
screen.best_lead_title: Phase diagram and high-resolution photoemission study of the superconducting and magnetic pseudoternary body-centered-tetragonal Ho(Rh1-xRux)4B4 system

screen.reason: This is ThCr2Si2-type ErFe2Ge2. Malik et al. (AIP Conf. Proc. 1976) report it as paramagnetic between 4.2 and 273 K. Szytula et al. (JMMM 2010) studied its magnetic ordering and low-temperature thermodynamics. Avila, Bud'ko and Canfield (JMMM 2003) measured RFe2Ge2 single crystals for magnetisation, specific heat and resistivity. In this family, superconductivity is reported only for non-magnetic YFe2Ge2 (about 1.8 K, Zou et al. 2014; Chen et al. 2016), and no paper I found reports it for ErFe2Ge2.
screen.best_lead_title: Magnetic ordering and low-temperature thermodynamic properties of ErFe2Ge2

screen.reason: This is ZrSb2. The only physical-property study I found, Sun et al. (EPL 120, 37002, 2017) on single crystals of alpha-ZrSb2, reports metallic behaviour, T^3 resistivity below 30 K, Kohler's-rule magnetoresistance and hole-type Hall carriers, with no mention of superconductivity. The superconducting Zr-Sb rows in the table are the Zr-rich phases: Zr5Sb3 at 2.3 K (Lv et al., PRB 2013) and Zr3Sb below 1 K (Willis et al. 1978). These lie more than 25 at.% away and are different phases. Soheilnia et al. (2003) also show that the reported 'beta-ZrSb2' is actually a Si- or Ge-stabilised ternary phase.
screen.best_lead_title: Crystal growth and magneto-transport properties of alpha-ZrSb2 and alpha-HfSb2
other_leads: Soheilnia, Assoud, Kleinke, Inorg. Chem. 2003, 'MA(delta)Sb(2-delta) (M = Zr, Hf; A = Si, Ge): a new series of ternary antimonides and not beta-ZrSb2' (DOI not retrieved)

screen.reason: This is the H-phase (211 MAX phase) V2AlC. Searches by formula and as a MAX phase with 'superconduct' found structural, transport and MXene-precursor papers (for example Etzkorn et al., Inorg. Chem. 2007), and none reports superconductivity in V2AlC. The superconducting 211 phases in the literature are Nb-based (Nb2SnC, Nb2InC, Bortolozo et al.). The SuperCon null probably comes from the 1960s survey of complex carbides by Toth, Jeitschko and Yen (J. Less-Common Met. 10, 1966). That paper has no abstract online, and I did not read it.
screen.best_lead_title: The superconducting behavior of several complex carbides and nitrides

screen.reason: The fractions give V3Al2C, the V analogue of the filled beta-Mn superconductor Mo3Al2C. Searches for V3Al2C and for V-Al-C carbides with 'superconduct' found no paper reporting this composition as a superconductor. The filled beta-Mn phase papers (Jeitschko, Nowotny and Benesovsky 1964) and the carbide superconductivity surveys of that period report Mo3Al2C, not a V analogue. The null most likely comes from the same 1960s complex-carbide survey as V2AlC (Toth et al. 1966), which I could not read. Whether a single-phase V3Al2C even exists is unconfirmed.
screen.best_lead_title: The superconducting behavior of several complex carbides and nitrides

screen.reason: This is a slightly off-stoichiometric UPd2Al3, a heavy-fermion superconductor with Tc about 2 K. The arithmetic fits a nominal UPd2Al2.97 (U 1/5.97 = 0.1675, Pd 0.3350, Al 0.4975), but that formula is my inference, not something I read. The table's neighbouring rows, 0.1 to 0.5 at.% away, are all superconducting (0.61 to 1.94 K) and match nominal UPd2+xAl3+y samples. Two groups measured such series: Schank et al. (J. Alloys Compd. 1994) on the effect of off-stoichiometry in UNi2Al3 and UPd2Al3, and Sato and Sakon et al. (Physica B 1993-94; IEEE Trans. Magn. 1994). Both abstracts say the properties are very sensitive to stoichiometry but give no per-sample Tc. Only the tables or figures can show whether this sample was measured as superconducting or as a null; the three zero reports in the table may well reflect a measured null.
screen.best_lead_title: Influence of off-stoichiometry on the properties of the heavy fermion superconductors UNi2Al3 and UPd2Al3

reader_a.evidence_note: The lead paper (Schank, Jahrling, Grauel, Borth, Helfrich, Luhmann, Reinders, Geibel, Steglich 1994) studied deviations from stoichiometry in UPd2Al3 and reports in its abstract that they reduce Tc while leaving TN unchanged. The abstract names no composition and no Tc value, so it cannot support route STATED, and with no sample list it cannot support route BRACKETED. The other leads (Sato et al. IEEE Trans. Magn. 30 (1994) 1145, 10.1109/20.312209; Sakon et al. Physica B 199-200 (1994) 154, 10.1016/0921-4526(94)91766-3; Sato et al. Physica B 186-188 (1993) 195, 10.1016/0921-4526(93)90532-b) use the nominal formula UPd2+xAl3+y for single crystals; their abstracts (read via OpenAlex and SciSpace records) name only UPd2Al3, UPd2Al3.03 and UPd2.02Al3.03, none of which is this row, and give no Tc for an Al-deficient or Pd-rich sample. Which paper the SuperCon entry for this row came from is not established. Because off-stoichiometry is reported to reduce Tc, it is also possible that the source sample did not superconduct above the lowest temperature reached; nothing read here settles either way.

The superconducting x = 0.3 row in the table comes from somewhere else, and nothing I found brackets x = 0.6 with superconducting samples.

refutation_attempts: Source re-read: Oka et al., PRL 108, 047001 (2012), full text of arXiv:1107.2711v2 (opened with curl, pdftotext). The deciding statements are as the readers quoted: p.1 'Bulk superconductivity sets in at Tc = 21 K for x = 0.04, with strong AFSF.' and 'ac susceptibility measurements using the in-situ NQR coil indicate Tc = 21, 27, 23, 18, and 12 K for x = 0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10, and 0.15'. p.4 Table I gives Tc = 21 K for 0.04(L) and 0.04(H). The readers read the paper correctly.

Arithmetic: LaFeAsO0.96F0.04 has 4.00 atoms per formula unit, giving La = Fe = As = 0.2500, O = 0.2400 and F = 0.0100. This matches the row exactly on paper. But x is nominal: p.1 says 'x indicates the nominal composition of the starting material'. The 0.15 at.% limit on F equals a tolerance of 0.006 in x.

Is nominal x a reliable measure of composition here? No. Oka et al. p.2: '...the nu_Q is quite similar to ours although the nominal x there is larger than ours by ~0.02'. Ref. [22] there is Lang et al., PRL 104, 097001 (2010), which used IFW Dresden samples. So Oka's nominal x = 0.04 sample matches, by NQR frequency, a Dresden sample of nominal x of about 0.06. The offset of 0.02 in x is 0.5 at.% F, more than three times the 0.15 at.% limit. Kondrat et al. (WDX, same Dresden source) state that 'for x <= 0.04 the actual F-contents are somewhat smaller than the nominal doping levels'. Neither superconducting paper (Oka; Nakai) reports a measured F content.

Later work by the same group: Yang, Oka, Li, ..., Chen, Zheng, Sci. China Phys. Mech. Astron. (2018), DOI 10.1007/s11433-018-9240-0, arXiv:1707.04085 (read). It now reports bulk superconductivity at nominal x = 0.03 (Tc = 9.5 K, coexisting with AF order). The 2012 PRL described x = 0.03 only as antiferromagnetic (TN = 58 K), with superconductivity setting in at x = 0.04. The 2018 abstract says the first dome 'appears at 0.03 <= x <= 0.2'. On this group's nominal scale, superconductivity starts about 0.02 lower than in the Dresden series. That is the same offset, and it confirms that a nominal x near the boundary does not fix the actual composition.

Bulk and ambient pressure: Oka's samples are bulk polycrystals, measured without applied pressure, and their synthesis was at ambient pressure (the 2018 paper says the 'AP method' was used for x = 0.03-0.2). No objection here.

Phase purity: Oka's x = 0.04 sample shows two 75As NQR sites, which the authors call phase separation, as in the antiferromagnetic x = 0.03 sample. Both sites show the 1/T1 drop at 21 K, so no foreign phase carries the superconductivity. Still, the sample sits on the AF/SC boundary.

Second positive paper (reader A): Nakai et al., JPSJ 77, 073701 (2008), arXiv:0804.4765 (read). Polycrystalline La(O1-xFx)FeAs, Hosono-group samples: 'Tc for x =0.04 and 0.11 determined from the onset of the SC transition with ac susceptibility is 17.5 K and 22.7 K'. x is again nominal and F content is not measured. The Hosono group's own discovery paper, Kamihara et al., JACS 130, 3296 (2008), DOI 10.1021/ja800073m (title and abstract via FastTrack get_paper; full text paywalled, not read), gives the superconducting range in its title as 'x = 0.05-0.12'.

Contrary reports for the same nominal composition (both found and read, see contrary_reports): Kondrat et al., EPJB 70, 461 (2009), and Luetkens et al., Nature Materials 8, 305 (2009), which use the same IFW Dresden sample series. Both report bulk nominal LaO0.96F0.04FeAs at ambient pressure as not superconducting. Its ground state is a long-range SDW with 100% magnetic volume. Superconductivity appears abruptly at x = 0.05; a related Dresden NMR paper (Hammerath et al., PRB 88, 104503, 2013, abstract seen in search only) lists x = 0.045 as its lowest superconducting sample. These are very likely where the table's zero comes from (SuperCon records nominal compositions).

The label for nominal x = 0.04 is therefore contested between groups rather than shown to be wrong, and under the rule's 'when in doubt' clause I do not apply it.

refutation_attempts: DOI check: FastTrack verify_reference on 10.1088/0953-8984/26/42/425701 returned a Crossref-registered journal article: Li, Luo, Li, Chen, Xu, Dai, Yang, Zhang, Cao, Xu, 'Kramers non-magnetic superconductivity in LnNiAsO superconductors', J. Phys.: Condens. Matter 26(42) 425701 (2014). FastTrack get_paper and the OpenAlex record carry no retraction flag. The second lead, 10.1088/0953-2048/25/8/084017 (Matsuishi et al., Supercond. Sci. Technol. 25, 084017, 2012), is also registered with Crossref.

Deciding statement re-read: the abstract names PrNiAsO and gives Tc = 0.93 K. It also says the superconductivity of PrNiAsO was further studied by upper critical field and specific heat measurements, which 'reveal that PrNiAsO is a weakly coupled Kramers non-magnetic superconductor'. Both readers quoted this text correctly.

Arithmetic: PrNiAsO = Pr1 Ni1 As1 O1, 4 atoms per formula unit, so each element is 1/4 = 0.2500. The row has As 0.250, Ni 0.250, O 0.250, Pr 0.250, so the difference is 0.000 on every element (limit 0.0015). This holds.

Bulk or film: the abstract describes a series of LnNiAsO compounds (Ln = La, Ce, Pr, Nd, Sm) and a specific heat measurement of the superconductivity. Specific heat is a bulk thermodynamic probe, and nothing in the abstract or keywords points to a film or nanostructure. The sample form (polycrystal or crystal) is not stated in the abstract.

Pressure: the abstract and its OpenAlex keywords ('superconducting transition temperature', 'upper critical field', 'specific heat', 'weak coupling', 'conventional superconductivity') mention no applied pressure. The study compares ground states across rare-earth substitution, not under pressure. Ambient pressure is inferred from that; the abstract does not say it in words. The Matsuishi samples were made by high-pressure synthesis, which is a growth route; the rule excludes superconductivity that exists only under applied pressure, which nothing indicates here.

Phase purity and impurity attribution: phase purity cannot be checked without the full text. I looked for a superconducting impurity in the Pr-Ni-As-O system that could explain a transition near 0.9 K and found none among the papers I opened. Pr20Ni42As31 orders antiferromagnetically at 11 K (Babizhetskyy et al., PRB 66, 014102, 2002, abstract). R3Ni4As4O2-delta superconducts only for R = La (Wang et al., PRB 89, 094405, 2014, abstract). RE2(Cu1-xNix)5As3O2 superconducts for Pr only with mixed Cu/Ni, up to about 60% Ni (Chen et al., iScience 2019, abstract). The authors attribute the transition to PrNiAsO and back it with specific heat and Hc2 measurements. A second, independent group (Hosono's group, Matsuishi et al. 2012) also reports PrNiAsO as superconducting, at Tc = 1.6 K (abstract re-read this session through FastTrack get_paper).

Discrepancy between reports: Tc is 0.93 K in Li et al. 2014 and 1.6 K in Matsuishi et al. 2012. The Matsuishi samples were made at high pressure with PrH2 in the starting mixture, and up to 18% of the O sites can carry H in that route, so the two samples may differ in H content or stoichiometry. Both groups call PrNiAsO a superconductor. The difference is in Tc, not in whether it superconducts.

Contrary-report searches: FastTrack search_papers ('PrNiAsO nickel oxyarsenide'; 'LnNiAsO rare earth nickel arsenide oxide superconductivity Pr'; 'nickel-based oxypnictide superconductor LaNiAsO rare earth substitution Pr Nd Tc'; 'rare-earth nickel arsenide oxides RNiAsO magnetic and transport properties'); FastTrack get_citations on the Li et al. DOI (8 citing works, none reporting PrNiAsO as non-superconducting); SciSpace search on whether PrNiAsO has been found non-superconducting; two WebSearch queries ('PrNiAsO superconductivity'; 'PrNiAsO not superconducting OR non-superconducting nickel oxyarsenide'); arxiv.org search pages for PrNiAsO, NiAsO, LnNiAsO, PrNiPO, 'Kramers non-magnetic superconductivity' and 'nickel-based oxyarsenides'. None of these turned up a report that PrNiAsO was measured below 0.93 K and found not superconducting.

Other papers opened for context: the Hosono and Matsuishi review (arXiv 1304.7900, full text) discusses LnNiAsO1-xHx and says the Tc of LaNiAsO is lowered by isovalent substitution of La with Ce, Pr or Nd. It gives no contrary null for PrNiAsO. Luo et al., Nature Materials 2014 on CeNiAsO (arXiv 1408.3132, full text) does not mention PrNiAsO. Two arXiv hits from the web search (0807.4872 and 0904.1570) are about PrFeAsO, a different compound.

Where the table's zero may come from: I could not find the SuperCon source record from here. One plausible source is a measurement that stopped at about 1.8-2 K, the usual lower limit of a standard cryostat, which would be above Tc = 0.93 K and would not contradict it. Another is a mis-entry. This is a guess, not something a document I read shows.

sceptic.verifier_reason: I re-read the Li et al. (2014) abstract myself. I checked its DOI against Crossref with FastTrack verify_reference and found no retraction flag. The abstract states superconductivity in PrNiAsO with Tc = 0.93 K and backs it with specific heat and upper critical field measurements. The formula matches the row exactly: 0.250 for each of the four elements. Nothing in the abstract points to a film, nanostructure or applied pressure. I found no superconducting impurity in the Pr-Ni-As-O system that could explain the transition, and an independent group (Matsuishi et al. 2012, re-read) also reports PrNiAsO as a superconductor. My searches of FastTrack, citing works, SciSpace, the web and arXiv found no paper reporting PrNiAsO as non-superconducting below 0.93 K, and no later correction. Three caveats come from reading only the abstract: the Tc criterion, the lowest measured temperature and phase purity are not stated, and ambient pressure is inferred rather than stated. These are gaps in detail. They give no reason of substance to doubt that bulk PrNiAsO superconducts at ambient pressure, so under the owner's rule (option B for abstracts) the correction applies.

refutation_attempts: Source re-read. I opened all 8 pages of Dmitriev et al., Acta Phys. Pol. A 114 (2008) 83-90 as text myself. The alphaXiv PDF reader fetched https://przyrbwn.icm.edu.pl/APP/PDF/114/a114z111.pdf; no Firecrawl credits were used. The deciding statement is the Fig. 1 caption on p. 85: 'Inset in Fig. 1a shows the resistivity superconducting transition for DyRh4B4 with TC onset ≈ 4.7 K.' On p. 87 the text names 'superconducting samples DyRh4B4 and Dy0.8Y0.2Rh4B4' and says the heat capacity of the Dy samples shows superconducting phase transitions besides the AFM transitions. The figures themselves could not be viewed, only their captions and the text.

Arithmetic. DyRh4B4 has 9 atoms: Dy 1/9 = 0.11111, Rh 4/9 = 0.44444, B 4/9 = 0.44444. Against the row (Dy 0.111, Rh 0.444, B 0.444) the differences are 0.0001, 0.0004 and 0.0004. All are under the 0.0015 limit. The paper gives only the nominal formula (x = 0 of Dy1-xYxRh4B4) and no microprobe composition.
Bulk or film. Bulk. The paper's samples are polycrystalline conglomerates of 3-10 um crystallites. Measured pieces were 2x2x1 mm3 for point contact and 1x1x5 mm3 for resistivity (p. 84).

Pressure. The measurements were made at ambient pressure: a four-probe system, a Quantum Design SQUID, a PPMS and a relaxation calorimeter, with no pressure cell mentioned. The phase, however, is made by high-pressure synthesis. Terekhov et al. (arXiv 1507.03247, full text read) say Dy1-xYxRh4B4 'gain the required structure only during the synthesis under a pressure of 8 GPa'. This is a metastable bct (LuRu4B4-type) phase quenched to and measured at ambient pressure. It is not superconductivity under pressure, so the rule's pressure exclusion does not apply.

Phase purity and the origin of the superconductivity. The paper says XRD, electron diffraction and optics show single-phase LuRu4B4-type samples. Koehler et al. 2009 (arXiv 0905.4032, full text read) argue that the 37-40 K magnetic transition in the high-pressure DyRh4B4 comes from a DyRh3B2 impurity, so the single-phase claim may be overstated. That impurity is magnetic, not a superconductor; the project's own table lists DyRh3B2 (B:0.333;Dy:0.167;Rh:0.500) as not a superconductor. Three further sources tie a Tc near 4-4.7 K to bct-DyRh4B4 itself. Koehler et al., a different group, attribute the 4.4 K superconductivity in their Si-added samples to bct-DyRh4B4, with about 50% superconducting volume fraction in DyRh4B4Si0.2. They also cite Johnston 1977: bct Dy(Rh0.85Ru0.15)4B4 has Tc about 4.0 K. Zaleski et al. 2006 (abstract) report Tc = 4.5 K for x = 0 from AC and DC magnetization, with Meissner behaviour. The heat-capacity text in Dmitriev indicates a bulk transition. I found no superconducting impurity that could explain a 4.5-4.7 K transition.

Partial drop. Not the case: the authors call it the superconducting transition of DyRh4B4. Magnetization gives Tc 4.5 K (Zaleski 2006 abstract; Burkhanov 2013 abstract, 'DyRh4B4 (samples HP) with Tc ≈ 4.5 K').

Later corrections. FastTrack get_citations on 10.12693/aphyspola.114.83 lists 14 citing works. None is a correction, erratum or refutation. They are mostly the same group's follow-ups on Dy1-xYxRh4B4 and Dy(Rh,Ru)4B4, and Terekhov et al. 2025 (arXiv 2503.07024, read in part) repeat 'Tc ... from 4,7 K for DyRh4B4'. The DOI is registered with Crossref (FastTrack verify_reference) and carries no retraction flag.

Where the table's zero probably comes from. The common, arc-melted primitive-tetragonal (CeCo4B4-type) DyRh4B4 is a ferromagnet with TM about 12 K. Koehler et al. 2009 measured their Si-free as-cast DyRh4B4: AC susceptibility shows only ferromagnetism below 12.3 K, with no diamagnetic superconducting signal in the plotted range of about 2-50 K, and a hysteresis loop at 2 K (Fig. 2). Matthias et al. 1977 (PNAS 74, 1334) reported the RRh4B4 series as either ferromagnetic or superconducting; only its abstract was seen, and it does not name Dy. Those zeros belong to a different polymorph. They do not contradict superconductivity in the bct polymorph of the same composition.
contrary_reports: Koehler, Behr, Fuchs, Nenkov, Gupta, J. Alloys Compd. (2009), doi 10.1016/j.jallcom.2009.04.040 (arXiv 0905.4032, full text read). Arc-melted (pt) DyRh4B4 without Si: ferromagnetic below 12.3 K, no superconducting signal reported, AC susceptibility plotted down to about 2 K. This is the primitive-tetragonal polymorph, not the high-pressure bct phase.

Matthias, Corenzwit, Vandenberg, Barz, PNAS 74, 1334 (1977), doi 10.1073/pnas.74.4.1334. This is the probable origin of the ferromagnetic, non-superconducting entry for pt-DyRh4B4. Not opened (PMC and pnas.org fetches failed). Its abstract does not name Dy or give a lowest temperature.

No report found of bct (high-pressure) DyRh4B4 measured as non-superconducting. Searches run: FastTrack search_papers 'DyRh4B4 superconductivity ferromagnetism rare earth rhodium borides', 'high pressure synthesis LuRu4B4-type DyRh4B4 YRh4B4 superconductivity', 'DyRh4B4 ferromagnet 12 K not superconducting CeCo4B4-type'; FastTrack get_citations on the Dmitriev DOI; an arXiv search for 'DyRh4B4' (only 0905.4032 found). An OpenAlex keyword search was refused because the daily budget was used up.

sceptic.verifier_reason: I re-read the full text of Dmitriev et al. 2008 (doi 10.12693/APhysPolA.114.83; verified with Crossref, no retraction flag). It states a resistive superconducting transition for DyRh4B4 with Tc onset about 4.7 K (Fig. 1 caption, p. 85) and names DyRh4B4 a superconducting sample on p. 87. The formula matches the row within 0.0004 on every element. The samples are mm-size bulk polycrystals measured with standard ambient-pressure apparatus. High pressure (about 8 GPa) was used only to make the metastable bct phase. I tried four routes to refute this. (1) Phase purity: Koehler et al. 2009 doubt the single-phase claim and point to a DyRh3B2 impurity, but that phase is magnetic and not superconducting. An independent group's Si-stabilised bct-DyRh4B4 (4.4 K) and bct Dy(Rh0.85Ru0.15)4B4 (4.0 K) put the superconductivity in the bct DyRh4B4 phase. (2) Pressure: the superconductivity is not under pressure. (3) Corrections: none among the 14 citing works. (4) Contrary reports: all concern the primitive-tetragonal arc-melted polymorph, a 12 K ferromagnet, not the sample in this paper. None of these is a reason of substance to doubt that DyRh4B4, as a bulk sample at ambient pressure, superconducts in its bct form, so the STATED route stands and I apply. Caveat for the auditor: superconductivity at this composition depends on the polymorph and needs high-pressure synthesis. The common arc-melted DyRh4B4 does not superconduct.

reader_a.synthesis_conditions: Nd2S3, SrF2, Bi and S weighed for Sr0.5Nd0.5FBiS2 and pelletized; sintered in an evacuated quartz tube at 700 C for 20 h and furnace cooled; reground and sintered again under the same conditions.
reader_a.quote: This is the first study to report on the observation of superconductivity in Sr0.5Nd0.5FBiS2 and Sr0.5Sm0.5FBiS2 under ambient pressure. However, in these samples, the estimated shielding volume fraction was less than 6%.
reader_a.evidence_note: Yamashita et al. (Sci. Rep. 2020; arXiv:2006.08489v1) measured a bulk polycrystalline sample of nominal Sr0.5Nd0.5FBiS2 at ambient pressure. They report a superconducting transition at Tc = 2.6 K: resistivity drops to zero (Fig. 3 inset) and magnetization shows a small diamagnetic step (Fig. 4). The abstract adds: 'This indicated the non-bulk nature of superconductivity in these samples under ambient pressure.' On p.3, bulk superconductivity is something they obtain only by applying pressure ('To obtain bulk superconductivity ... we applied external pressure on the samples'). On p.4 they count 20% shielding or more as bulk; the ambient-pressure state falls in the 'filamentary superconductivity' region. In Fig. 4 the Nd ZFC magnetization stays positive (paramagnetic background) down to about 1.8 K, with only a small drop. Contrary report, same nominal composition: Jha, Tiwari and Awana, J. Appl. Phys. 117, 013901 (2015), DOI 10.1063/1.4905391 (arXiv:1407.3105, full text read). They write that 'the Nd, Pr and Sm samples are not superconducting down to 2K' at ambient pressure: their Sr0.5Nd0.5FBiS2 is semiconducting from 2 to 300 K and superconducts only under pressure, up to about 10 K at 1.5-2.5 GPa. Because the two reports conflict, I do not give verified_null either.
reader_a.reason_if_not: Route STATED is not met without stretching. The sample is a bulk polycrystal at ambient pressure, its nominal formula matches the row exactly, and the authors call the 2.6 K transition superconductivity. But they state that this superconductivity is non-bulk (filamentary, shielding volume fraction below 6%) and that bulk superconductivity appears only under hydrostatic pressure, and superconductivity under pressure does not confirm. Two further points weaken the case. The sample's measured EDX composition, Sr0.60Nd0.39FBi0.98S2.03, is 2.0-2.2 at.% away from the row on Sr and Nd. An independent sample of the same nominal composition (Jha et al. 2015) showed no superconductivity down to 2 K at ambient pressure. If the owner decides that filamentary superconductivity with zero resistance in a bulk polycrystalline sample, at the nominal composition, meets 'superconductivity ... in a bulk sample', this paper would satisfy route STATED with Tc = 2.6 K. That is the owner's call, not mine. Route BRACKETED does not apply: there is no composition series.

refutation_attempts: Deciding statement: re-read p. 176 (Introduction) myself. It lists ScSe, Tc = 3.7 K, among new NaCl-structure superconductors discovered in this work. The abstract on p. 175 also says: 'Binary compounds found to be superconducting are ThS, ScSe, ThSe, HfP, and ThP.' Both readers quoted this correctly. The quote above is my plain-text rendering of the preview's math markup.

Composition arithmetic: the paper writes ScSe, so Sc = 1/2 = 0.500 and Se = 1/2 = 0.500. The row is Sc 0.500, Se 0.500. Both differences are 0.000, within the 0.0015 limit. The same sentence spells out off-stoichiometric phases where they apply (Zr1-xS, Sc1-xS, YSx) but writes the selenide as plain ScSe, so the paper states the 1:1 compound. Caveat: the analysed composition and vacancy content of the ScSe sample are in the unread body. The paper stresses that NaCl-type phases in this family can carry large vacancy concentrations.

Bulk or film: the paper studies bulk NaCl-structure binary and pseudobinary compounds. The abstract and introduction mention specific heat, room-temperature susceptibility, resistance, solid-solution synthesis and high-pressure Tc. Neither page mentions films or nanostructures.

Pressure: the introduction lists the discovery Tc values, ScSe 3.7 K among them, and then says separately that 'Tc as a function of pressure was obtained for many of these compounds'. The listed 3.7 K is therefore the zero-applied-pressure value. The ScSe experimental section was not read.

Phase purity and impurity: the authors attribute the transition to the ScSe compound itself. Neither constituent element superconducts near 3.7 K at ambient pressure: Sc superconducts only under high pressure, as the abstracts of Debessai et al. PRB 2008 and Hamlin's Sc pressure studies, seen in search results, state. No known Sc-Se phase is a 3.7 K superconductor. I could not check the X-ray phase analysis. Unresolvable check: 3.7 K is close to the Tc of tin (3.72 K), but nothing in the pages read suggests tin was in contact with the sample, so this is not evidence against the report. Someone reading the full paper should check the sample-preparation route.

The deciding statement is on p.4: 'As x further increases to 0.4, resistivity shows semiconducting behavior before a sharp superconducting transition with Tconset ... ∼ 2.0 K sets up'. Fig. 2(b) (p.8), which I viewed myself, shows the x = 0.4 curve peaking near 38 mOhm cm at about 2.5 K, about 37 at 2.0 K, about 21 at 1.6 K, about 4 at 1.2 K and zero below about 1.1 K. Both readers quoted and located this correctly.

Composition arithmetic: Sr0.6La0.4FBiS2 has 5 atoms per formula unit; Sr 0.6/5 = 0.120, La 0.4/5 = 0.080, F 0.200, Bi 0.200, S 0.400. Exact match to the row (difference 0.000 on every element). The formula is nominal; Li reports EDX on single grains as 'very close to the nominal' with no numbers, so the real La content is not known to within the 0.0075 in x that 0.15 at.% La corresponds to.

Bulk / ambient / phase: Li's sample is a bulk polycrystal from solid-state reaction, measured with no applied pressure (PPMS with 3He insert, to 0.4 K). Li states that x = 0.4 alone is single phase by XRD (p.3), so no known superconducting impurity explains the drop. But the bulk nature of superconductivity at x = 0.4 is not shown: the susceptibility in Fig. 3 covers only x = 0.5, 0.55, 0.6, 0.7, and its temperature axis starts at 2.0 K (MPMS-5), at or above the x = 0.4 onset, so the text's 'for all superconducting samples, strong diamagnetic signals are observed' cannot have covered the x = 0.4 transition. The x = 0.4 claim rests on resistivity alone, in a sample at the insulator-superconductor boundary where a percolating minority of more heavily doped grains could give zero resistance.

Contrary report found and read in full: Sakai et al., J. Phys. Soc. Jpn. 83, 014709 (2014), arXiv 1311.5117. Their own bulk polycrystal of nominal x = 0.4, measured at ambient pressure, shows resistivity still rising down to about 1.8 K (Fig. 4b, p.10, which I viewed), no diamagnetic signal (Fig. 4a), and no specific-heat anomaly from about 1.8 K to 5 K (Fig. 7, p.15). Text p.9: 'With decreasing x from 0.45, Tc rapidly drops and a clear superconducting transition disappears for x=0.4.' Fig. 5(a) (p.11) plots x = 0.4 at Tc = 0 on the insulator side. If Sakai's sample behaved like Li's, its resistivity at 1.8 K would already be about 25% below the normal-state value; it is not, so the two samples of the same nominal composition genuinely disagree, not just in how low each group measured.

Where the table's zero comes from: Sakai's Fig. 5(a) data points match the same-system rows in the task file (x = 0.42, La 0.084, midpoint Tc about 2.1 K vs table 2.13 K; x = 0.45, La 0.090, about 3.1 K vs 3.1 K; x = 0.6, La 0.120, about 2.95 K vs 2.96 K; x = 0.25, La 0.050, Tc = 0 vs table zero). The table's zero for x = 0.4 therefore very likely comes from Sakai's x = 0.4 point, a real primary measurement, not a data-entry error. Li's series (x = 0.55, 0.7) does not appear among the same-system rows, so Li's paper seems not to have been entered at all.

sceptic.verifier_reason: The readers' reading of Li et al. is accurate: the paper states a superconducting transition (onset about 2.0 K, zero resistance near 1.1 K in Fig. 2b) for nominal Sr0.6La0.4FBiS2, an exact at.% match, in a bulk single-phase polycrystal at ambient pressure. It nevertheless fails the sceptic test because there is a reason of substance to doubt that this composition superconducts as a bulk sample at ambient pressure. An independent, careful primary study, Sakai et al. (JPSJ 83, 014709, 2014), made a bulk polycrystal of the same nominal composition and measured it at ambient pressure with resistivity, susceptibility and specific heat. It found no transition down to about 1.8 K and placed x = 0.4 on the insulating side with Tc = 0. That is where Li's sample should already show a clear drop, so the two samples disagree outright. The table's zero almost certainly comes from that measurement, so the zero is a genuine primary report, not an entry error. The composition sits on a steep insulator-superconductor boundary where Tc changes from 0 to about 2 K within a few hundredths in x. That is smaller than the uncertainty in the real La content of either sample: both are nominal, and Li's EDX gives no numbers. Li's own bulk evidence for x = 0.4 is resistivity alone; its susceptibility figure omits x = 0.4 and does not go below 2.0 K. With one positive and one negative primary report for the same nominal composition, the label is sample dependent and not shown to be wrong, so the correction is not applied.

reader_b.evidence_note: He et al., 'Superconductivity in Pd-intercalated charge-density-wave rare earth poly-tellurides RETen', arXiv:1301.3032 (published as Supercond. Sci. Technol. 29, 065018 (2016), DOI 10.1088/0953-2048/29/6/065018, Crossref-verified; OpenAlex links the arXiv id to it). The PdxHoTe3 series measured is x = 0, 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10, 0.14, 0.16, 0.18 (Fig. 2b legend). The x=0.10 curve in Fig. 2b falls from a normal-state plateau of about 1.12 (rho/rho380K) to zero between about 2.6 and 2.45 K; the same sample shows a ZFC diamagnetic signal in Fig. 3a reaching roughly -0.02 emu/g/Oe at 1.8 K, comparable to the x=0.08 curve for which the authors estimate 100% shielding. The paper's series ends at x=0.18 and contains no x=0.2 or x=0.4 HoTe3 sample, so the table's other same-system rows (HoPd0.2Te3, HoPd0.4Te3) do not correspond to samples in this preprint.

sceptic.re_read_source_url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1301.3032 (v1, 14 Jan 2013, the only version on the abstract page; 27 pages; text extracted with pdftotext, figure pages 21, 22, 23 and 27 rendered and viewed)
sceptic.at_pct_check: Pd0.10HoTe3: 1 + 0.10 + 3 = 4.10 atoms per formula unit. Ho = 100/4.10 = 24.390 at.%, Pd = 10/4.10 = 2.439 at.%, Te = 300/4.10 = 73.171 at.%. Row: Ho 24.4, Pd 2.4, Te 73.2 at.%. Differences: Ho 0.010, Pd 0.039, Te 0.029 at.%; all within 0.15 at.%. Neighbours in the same series: x = 0.08 is Pd 1.961 at.% (0.48 at.% away, outside the STATED limit, so it does not decide), x = 0.14 is Pd 3.382 at.%.
refutation_attempts: Composition: redid the arithmetic (above); only the x = 0.10 sample is within 0.15 at.% of the row. The formula is nominal (stoichiometric weighing); the paper reports no chemical analysis. Fig. 1d shows lattice parameter b rising steadily with x through x = 0.10, so the Pd does enter the lattice in step with the nominal x.

Superconductivity of x = 0.10 itself: Fig. 2b legend lists x = 0.10 (magenta left triangles); its normalized resistivity falls from about 1.12 to zero between about 2.6 K and 2.45 K. Fig. 3a (ZFC) shows a diamagnetic signal for x = 0.10 reaching about -0.024 emu/g/Oe at 1.8 K, close to the x = 0.08 sample for which the text estimates 100% shielding. Fig. 7 plots a closed (superconducting) circle at x = 0.10. My own pixel calibration of Fig. 7 (300 dpi; y ticks at 0 K and 2 K, 90.5 px/K) gives 2.62 K for x = 0.10; the same calibration gives 2.84 K for x = 0.08 against the 2.83 K stated in the text, and about 0 K for x = 0.02 (not superconducting).
Bulk or film: polycrystalline pellets made by solid-state reaction in sealed quartz; no films or nanostructures.
Pressure: no pressure cell or applied pressure anywhere in the text; measurements in PPMS and MPMS SQUID VSM. Ambient.

Phase purity / impurity origin: Fig. 1b shows no impurity arrows on the x = 0.10 XRD trace; Ho2Te5 arrows appear only on x = 0.18 (caption: impurity phases appear only for high doping). A Pd-Te impurity (PdTe, PdTe2) as the superconductor is unlikely: Tc changes systematically with x along a dome (2.55, 2.77, 2.84, 2.62, 2.50 K for x = 0.04 to 0.14 from Fig. 7), x = 0.02 does not superconduct, the CDW anomaly is suppressed in step, and the shielding is near full. Independent later work on flux-grown PdxHoTe3 single crystals (Lou et al., PRB 93, 115133) and on Pd-intercalated ErTe3 crystals (Fisher group, found by search) also reports superconductivity of the intercalated phase.

Where the table's zero may come from: Lou et al. (arXiv:1601.01564v2, opened) measured flux-grown PdxHoTe3 crystals with nominal x = 0, 0.01, 0.02, 0.04 and report SC at about 2.0 K (x = 0.02) and about 2.8 K (x = 0.04); its Fig. 1c shows no superconducting drop for x = 0.01. The table's positive neighbours HoPd0.2Te3 (Tc 2.0) and HoPd0.4Te3 (Tc 2.8) carry exactly Lou's Tc values at ten times Lou's x, so the zero row HoPd0.1Te3 is probably Lou's x = 0.01 crystal (Pd about 0.25 at.%) entered with x scaled by ten. Lou's own lattice parameters (Fig. 1a: b about 25.40 A at x = 0.04, about 25.345 A at x = 0.01) match He's polycrystal values near the same x, not at ten times x, so Lou's x = 0.01 crystal is not a Pd 2.4 at.% sample. I did not see the SuperCon source records; this is an inference, but it means the zero does not appear to be a measurement of this composition.

Later corrections: the arXiv abstract page shows v1 only and no withdrawal. The journal version, He et al., Supercond. Sci. Technol. 29, 065018 (2016), has 15 authors (4 more than the preprint); its full text is paywalled and was not read, so I could not check that x = 0.10 carried over unchanged. Its abstract (OpenAlex) gives no compositions and does not contradict the preprint. Lou et al. (2016) cite the preprint's polycrystal phase diagram without correction.

sceptic.verifier_reason: I re-read the full arXiv text and figures myself. The x = 0.10 member of He et al.'s PdxHoTe3 series, Pd0.10HoTe3, matches the row within 0.04 at.% on every element; it is a bulk polycrystalline pellet measured at ambient pressure; its resistivity falls to zero near 2.45 K (Fig. 2b), it shows strong ZFC diamagnetism comparable to the fully shielded x = 0.08 sample (Fig. 3a), and the paper's phase diagram (Fig. 7) plots its superconducting Tc at about 2.6 K. Its XRD shows no marked impurity, and the systematic Tc dome, the CDW suppression and the lattice expansion with x tie the superconductivity to the intercalated phase rather than to a Pd-Te impurity. I found no report of this composition being non-superconducting; the only other PdxHoTe3 transport study (Lou et al. 2016) measured crystals at Pd about 0.25-0.99 at.%, and the table's zero is best explained as its x = 0.01 crystal entered at ten times x. Residual limits, not of substance: the composition is nominal, Tc for x = 0.10 is read from a figure rather than stated in text, and the paywalled journal version was not read. The STATED route is met, so the 'not a superconductor' label should be corrected.

screen.reason: This is a Rh-rich fcc Rh-Ir-Os alloy (IrOs2Rh7). The table's own superconducting rows in this system (e.g. Ir0.125Os0.2Rh0.675, Tc 0.05 K; Ir0.1Os0.25Rh0.65, Tc 0.1 K) show Tc falling toward the Rh corner, and this row is the most Rh-rich point. No superconducting sample lies on its Rh-rich side, so a 2 at.% bracket is not possible. The likely source series are ultralow-temperature studies of Rh-rich alloys (Mota et al. 1971, 'Toward the superconductivity of rhodium') and Andres and Jensen 1968, whose abstract says strongly exchange-enhanced fcc alloys were not superconducting above their 0.015 K limit. A null at this composition is consistent with these leads, and no search hit reports it as superconducting.

reader_a.evidence_note: Rosa et al. 2014 (arXiv 1409.1287, read in full) report an In-flux BaFe1.9Cu0.1As2 single crystal with an ambient-pressure resistive Tc onset of 3.8 K. Piva et al. 2015 (JPCM 27, 145701, eScholarship copy, read in full) report ambient-pressure rho_ab for BaFe2-xCuxAs2 x = 0, 0.02, 0.09, 0.10, 0.11, 0.13 and state 'The SC samples present the onset ofTc varying from 2.5 to 4.2 K', with x_opd = 0.11. Ni et al. 2010 (arXiv 1006.3193, read in full) find, in self-flux Ba(Fe1-xCux)2As2, zero resistance only at x = 0.044 (offset 2.1 K, onset 2.2 K) and state 'superconductivity is not stabilized for T > 3 K'; their x = 0.05, 0.061 crystals show no superconductivity down to the 2 K base temperature. The task file's same-system rows (Cu/(Fe+Cu) = 0.0075, 0.021, 0.028, 0.036, 0.046, 0.051, 0.063, with Tc 2.15 K at 0.046) match Ni 2010's WDS series (0.0077, 0.02, 0.026, 0.035, 0.044, 0.05, 0.061), so this row is probably a SuperCon entry for Ni 2010's x = 0.05 crystal with an altered Fe count; this is an inference from the numbers, not a stated fact. So two groups disagree on whether Cu/(Fe+Cu) = 0.05 superconducts above 2 K (In-flux: yes, about 3.7-3.8 K resistive; self-flux: no down to 2 K).

BRACKETED fails because the row is not a member of the stoichiometric BaFe2-xCuxAs2 series (Ba 20.2 and As 40.4 at.% against 20.0 and 40.0 for every series sample). reader_b.quote: For sample with x = 0.1, the superconducting transition temperature (Tc) is around 1.7 K, which is consistent with the previous report36. For sample with x = 0.2, the Tc decreases apparently to 0.65 K.
reader_b.evidence_note: The paper reports measurements on the exact composition Ir0.8Pt0.2Te2 (x=0.2). Its R(T) drops completely to zero (Fig. 5a), the authors call this superconductivity and place x=0.2 inside the 'SC' dome of their phase diagram (Fig. 5c), and they measure Bc2 for the same sample (Fig. 5b). The sample is a bulk single crystal (mm-sized, normal-state resistance about 1.5 mOhm) and no pressure is applied. Caveats for the sceptic: (1) x appears to be nominal; EDS is shown only qualitatively. (2) The evidence is resistive only, with no susceptibility or specific heat. (3) The text does not say explicitly whether the transport piece was a whole crystal or a knife-cleaved piece, but the mOhm-scale resistance fits a bulk crystal, not a thin flake. (4) I read the arXiv v1 preprint (14 authors). The published Adv. Mater. version has 19 authors and I did not read it, so its numbers could differ. (5) The paper says earlier reports held that superconductivity is absent for x>0.1; its new result rests on dilution-refrigerator measurements below the temperatures those reports reached. That is a likely reason SuperCon carries zero entries for this composition.
reader_b.leads_for_library: Published version: Fei et al., Adv. Mater. 30(35), 1801556 (2018), DOI 10.1002/adma.201801556. Check that its main-text transport paragraph and R(T) figure still give Tc about 0.65 K for x=0.2, and see whether it adds measured (EDS/WDS) compositions or susceptibility data. Earlier reports cited for 'no superconductivity at x>0.1', to check for the lowest temperature they reached at x=0.2: Pyon, Kudo, Nohara, Physica C 494, 80-84 (2013); Fang et al., Sci. Rep. 3, 1153 (2013); Yang et al., PRL 108, 116402 (2012).

refutation_attempts: Source re-read: I downloaded arXiv:1711.10909 v1, the only version. It is the open-access copy that OpenAlex lists for DOI 10.1002/adma.201801556. I read the whole text with pdftotext and looked at Fig. 5 (p. 21) and Fig. 2 (p. 18) as images. The deciding sentence is on the superconductivity page (about p. 9): 'For sample with x = 0.2, the Tc decreases apparently to 0.65 K.' In Fig. 5a the green x = 0.2 curve falls from about 1.55 mOhm near 1 K to zero by about 0.6 K and is labelled 'Tc= 0.65K'. Fig. 5b gives Bc2(0) of about 263 Oe for x = 0.2, and Fig. 5c puts x = 0.2 inside the 'SC' dome.

Arithmetic: Ir0.8Pt0.2Te2 has 3 atoms per formula unit. That gives Ir 0.8/3 = 26.667, Pt 0.2/3 = 6.667 and Te 2/3 = 66.667 at.%. Against the row fractions (0.267/0.067/0.667) each element is 0.033 at.% off. Against the task's atomic_percent (26.67/6.69/66.63) the differences are Ir 0.003, Pt 0.023 and Te 0.037 at.%. All are within 0.15 at.%. Caveat: x is nominal. Methods give the flux ratio Ir:Pt:Te = 0.18(1-x):0.18x:0.82, and the EDS in Fig. 2b is qualitative only: Ir and Pt L-alpha peaks grow or shrink monotonically with x, but no analysed x is given. One cross-check comes from a different group (Fu et al., arXiv:1712.02500): their EDX of flux-grown crystals 'consistent with the corresponding nominal ones' (x = 0.1: Te 66.85, Ir 29.20, Pt 3.94 at.%). Both Fei (1.7 K) and Fu (about 2 K) find a similar Tc at nominal x = 0.1, so Fei's nominal scale does not appear grossly off.

Bulk or film: the samples are millimetre-sized hexagonal single crystals grown from Te self-flux, and no exfoliated flake or film is described for transport. A normal-state resistance of about 1.5 mOhm fits a bulk crystal, not a thin flake, which would show ohms.
Pressure: no pressure cell or applied pressure is mentioned. Transport was measured in a dilution refrigerator (lowest temperature stated as >47 mK), so the measurement is at ambient pressure.

Phase or impurity: XRD (shown for x = 0.4) fits single-phase 1T P-3m1. Fig. 2c R(T) for x = 0.1 to 0.4 shows no cooling/heating hysteresis, so there is no monoclinic/CDW transition. The transition goes completely to zero resistance, and the authors call it superconductivity of the sample. Tc falls smoothly across the series (1.7, 0.65 and 0.15 K at x = 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3), with matching Bc2 values (699, 263 and 27 Oe). Pt-poor IrTe2-like regions would superconduct at 1.7 to 3 K, not 0.65 K. Ir metal (about 0.1 K), Te and PtTe2 are not superconductors at 0.65 K at ambient pressure. I found no impurity that would explain a 0.65 K zero-resistance transition. Weakness: the evidence is resistive only, with no susceptibility or specific heat at x = 0.2.

Published version: the Adv. Mater. full text (19 authors, retitled) is paywalled, and the Wiley Scholar Gateway refused with 'free_tier_limit_reached', so I did not read it. Indirect check: Jiang et al., APL Mater. 8, 061106 (2020), DOI 10.1063/5.0011549 (CC BY), uses crystals from the same source and cites the Adv. Mater. paper as ref. 16 for growth. I read its full text through one Firecrawl scrape, and it repeats 'x = 0.2 (∼0.65 K)'. So the x = 0.2 value was not withdrawn after publication. That paper shares authors with Fei 2018 (Fei, Song), so it corroborates but is not independent.

Where the zero comes from: Pyon, Kudo and Nohara, JPSJ 81, 053701 (2012) (arXiv:1204.1421, read) studied polycrystalline Ir1-xPtxTe2 with 0 <= x <= 0.25. They state 'No trace of superconductivity was observed for x >= 0.10 down to 2.0 K', and their Fig. 1(b) caption says the bars mark 'the absence of bulk superconductivity above 2.0 K at x > 0'. That null reaches only 2.0 K, so it does not contradict a 0.65 K transition. It explains the table zeros for x = 0.10, 0.15, 0.20 and 0.25 in this series (two other groups find a Tc of about 1.7 to 2 K at x = 0.1, below that 2 K cutoff). Fei et al. also say earlier reports had 'Pt doping level ... far lower than our samples'.

Contrary searches: FastTrack forward citations of 10.1002/adma.201801556 (top 25), FastTrack searches ('Ir1-xPtxTe2 superconductivity Pt-doped IrTe2 low temperature phase diagram'; 'Ir0.8Pt0.2Te2 OR Ir0.7Pt0.3Te2 superconductivity'; 'Pt-doped IrTe2 single crystals heavily doped superconductivity absent'), and arXiv searches ('Ir1-xPtxTe2', 'Pt-doped IrTe2', 'IrPtTe2', 'Ir0.8Pt0.2Te2', 'PtxIr1-xTe2', 'Dirac fermions (Ir1-xPtx)Te2'). Kiswandhi et al. PRB 87, 121107 (arXiv:1212.5330) covers only x <= 0.05. The STM paper arXiv:1504.05295 has no low-temperature transport at x = 0.2. The closest contrary data point is Fu et al. (arXiv:1712.02500; Chin. Phys. B 28, 037103, 2019): 'the superconductivity does not appear at temperature above 0.3 K for x = 0.25' (He-3 resistivity, Fig. 2a). That is a different composition, 1.67 at.% Pt away from the row and outside the 0.15 at.% limit. It is in mild tension with Fei's dome, where linear interpolation gives about 0.4 K at x = 0.25, but it does not contradict x = 0.2. Fu et al. did not measure x = 0.2.

DOI check: FastTrack verify_reference confirms 10.1002/adma.201801556 is registered with Crossref (Fei et al., Adv. Mater. 30(35), 1801556, 2018, 19 authors), and OpenAlex get_work matches. Corroborating DOI 10.1063/5.0011549 is also registered (APL Mater. 8(6), 061106, 2020).
contrary_reports: No report found that measured Ir0.8Pt0.2Te2 (within 0.15 at.%) below 0.65 K and saw no superconductivity.

Pyon, Kudo, Nohara, J. Phys. Soc. Jpn. 81, 053701 (2012), doi:10.1143/JPSJ.81.053701 (arXiv:1204.1421, read): polycrystalline samples, no superconductivity for x >= 0.10 down to 2.0 K. This is the probable source of the table zero. It reaches only 2.0 K, above the 0.65 K Tc, so it is not a contradiction.

Fu et al., Chin. Phys. B 28, 037103 (2019), doi:10.1088/1674-1056/28/3/037103 (arXiv:1712.02500, read): no superconductivity above 0.3 K at x = 0.25 (Ir 25.0, Pt 8.33, Te 66.67 at.%). This is a different composition (Pt 1.67 at.% away) and not a null for this row. It is noted as mild tension at the Pt-rich edge of the dome.

Not checked (paywalled): Pyon, Kudo, Nohara, Physica C 494, 80 (2013), doi:10.1016/j.physc.2013.04.055 (single crystals). Fei et al. describe the earlier reports as having Pt levels 'far lower than our samples'.

No CDW/monoclinic transition in R(T) for x = 0.1 to 0.4. x is the nominal Ir:Pt ratio of the growth mix; EDS is qualitative only.

Mater. paper): superconductivity paragraph, about p. 9 ('For sample with x = 0.2, the Tc decreases apparently to 0.65 K.'); Fig. 5a (p. 21), x = 0.2 R(T) labelled 'Tc= 0.65K'; Fig. 5b (Bc2(0) about 263 Oe); Fig. 5c (phase diagram). Corroborated in Jiang et al., APL Mater. 8, 061106 (2020), doi:10.1063/5.0011549, experimental section: 'x = 0.2 (∼0.65 K)'.
sceptic.tc_criterion: Resistive. The value is the authors' label on Fig. 5a; the paper does not define the criterion. Read by eye from Fig. 5a: onset near 1 K, midpoint about 0.75 K, zero resistance at about 0.6 K. So 0.65 K sits near the zero-resistance end of the transition.
sceptic.measurement_method: Four-probe electrical resistance vs temperature in a dilution refrigerator (lowest temperature stated as >47 mK); upper critical field Bc2(T) from field-dependent resistance. No magnetization or specific heat at x = 0.2.
sceptic.synthesis_conditions: Te self-flux: Ir powder, Pt sponge and Te shot in atomic ratio 0.18(1-x):0.18x:0.82 in an alumina crucible, vacuum-sealed in a thick-walled ampoule; 950 C for 10 h, then 1160 C for 24 h, slowly cooled to 880 C over a week; Te flux removed by centrifugation.
sceptic.quote: For sample with x = 0.2, the Tc decreases apparently to 0.65 K.
sceptic.evidence_note: Fei et al. report a complete resistive transition to zero, called superconductivity by the authors, at Tc = 0.65 K in a bulk flux-grown single crystal of nominal Ir0.8Pt0.2Te2, at ambient pressure, with Bc2(0) of about 263 Oe. The result sits inside a systematic dome (x = 0.1: 1.7 K; 0.2: 0.65 K; 0.3: 0.15 K; 0.4: none above 47 mK). A 2020 published paper from overlapping authors (APL Mater., CC BY) restates x = 0.2 at about 0.65 K. The table's zero is best explained by Pyon et al. 2012, who measured only down to 2.0 K. Limitations: x is nominal, the evidence is resistive only, and only the arXiv preprint of the Adv. Mater. paper was read, not the published version.
sceptic.verifier_reason: I tried to refute the readers on composition, sample form, pressure, phase purity, published-version drift and contrary measurements, and none of these gives a reason of substance to doubt the row. The paper's formula Ir0.8Pt0.2Te2 matches the row within 0.04 at.% on every element. The sample is a millimetre-sized bulk single crystal measured at ambient pressure. The transition is complete, to zero resistance; the authors attribute it to the phase; it follows the doping trend with a matching Bc2; and no plausible impurity in the Ir-Pt-Te system superconducts at 0.65 K. The table's zero traces to a polycrystal study that stopped at 2.0 K. The only nearby null (Fu et al., x = 0.25, nothing above 0.3 K) is a different composition 1.67 at.% Pt away and is roughly consistent with a dome that falls to 0.15 K at x = 0.3. Remaining caveats: nominal x, transport only, and the published Adv. Mater. text not read. They are recorded, but they do not reach the owner's exclusions, and the 2020 APL Materials paper shows the x = 0.2 value was still stated after publication. Both readers confirmed by route STATED, and I re-read the source myself and could not refute it, so the correction applies.

screen.reason: This is Ir1-xPtxTe2 with x = 0.15 (Ir 28.33, Pt 5.0, Te 66.67 at.%). Fei et al. (Adv. Mater. 2018, arXiv 1711.10909, read in full) report superconductivity in single-phase 1T single crystals at x = 0.1 (Tc about 1.7 K) and x = 0.2 (Tc = 0.65 K), each 1.67 at.% from this row on Ir and Pt, so the BRACKETED route (within 2 at.% on both sides, all superconducting) appears to be met. refutation_attempts: Source re-read: downloaded arXiv:1711.10909 (v1, the only version) myself. Its abs page carries citation_doi 10.1002/adma.201801556. Read the superconductivity paragraph (PDF p. 9), Fig. 5a/5c (PDF p. 21), Fig. 2 and its text (PDF p. 6 and p. 18) and the Methods. The deciding statements are present as the readers quoted them: x = 0.1 Tc around 1.7 K, x = 0.2 Tc 0.65 K, x = 0.3 Tc 0.15 K, x = 0.4 no superconductivity above 47 mK. In Fig. 5a the resistances of x = 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 all fall to zero.

Arithmetic: Ir1-xPtxTe2 at x = 0.15 gives Ir 0.28333, Pt 0.05000, Te 0.66667, which matches the row within 0.04 at.%. The x = 0.1 sample (Ir 0.30000, Pt 0.03333) is 1.70 at.% Ir, 1.67 at.% Pt and 0.03 at.% Te from the row. The x = 0.2 sample (Ir 0.26667, Pt 0.06667) is 1.63 at.% Ir, 1.67 at.% Pt and 0.03 at.% Te from the row. So there is one superconducting sample on each side within 2 at.%, and the BRACKETED route holds. The next sample, x = 0.3, is 5 at.% away and is not needed.

Bulk and pressure: the samples are millimetre-sized Te self-flux single crystals (Methods; Fig. 2a inset), not films or nanoflakes. No pressure cell is mentioned and transport was measured in a dilution refrigerator, so the pressure is ambient.

Phase: the text says the P-3m1 fit indicates 'the pure 1T phase of Ir1-xPtxTe2 samples' (the XRD shown is x = 0.4 only). For x = 0.1-0.4 the cooling and heating R(T) curves coincide (Fig. 2c), which the authors take to mean no structural transition. I checked whether an impurity could carry the superconductivity. Te is not superconducting at ambient pressure. Pyon 2012 (read) reports no superconductivity in IrTe2 down to 0.32 K and in PtTe2 down to 1.2 K. Ir metal has Tc of about 0.1 K, far below 0.65 K. Pt-poor (x of about 0.03-0.08) inclusions would superconduct at 2-3 K, not at 0.65 K. The resistive Tc falls steadily with nominal x (1.7, 0.65, 0.15 K), and Hc2(0) falls with it (699, 263, 27 Oe, Fig. 5b). That is what a superconducting doped phase would show, not a fixed-Tc impurity. I found no sign that the superconductivity belongs to another compound.

Composition basis: Fei's x values are nominal flux-loading ratios, and the EDS (Fig. 2b inset) is qualitative only, though it shows the Pt L-alpha peak rising with x. An independent Te-flux growth of the same series, Fu et al. arXiv:1712.02500 (read), reports EDX compositions 'consistent with the corresponding nominal ones' for its crystals. Also, x = 0.15 lies between two superconducting members of one series, so a small composition offset would not put it outside a superconducting region unless the dome were non-monotonic, which none of the papers shows.

Published version: the published Adv. Mater. text could not be read (Wiley Scholar Gateway quota exhausted; the article is paywalled). The published abstract (OpenAlex, read) still says 'Superconductivity is also observed and persists when the Fermi level aligns with the Dirac points'. In arXiv v1 that alignment is at x = 0.3 (Tc 0.15 K), so the published version keeps superconductivity at least up to x = 0.3, beyond both bracketing samples.

Origin of the table's zero: Pyon, Kudo, Nohara 2012 (JPSJ 81, 053701; arXiv:1204.1421, read) Fig. 1(b) draws arrows at x = 0.10, 0.15, 0.20 and 0.25, which the caption says 'indicate the absence of bulk superconductivity above 2.0 K'. The text says 'No trace of superconductivity was observed for x >= 0.10 down to 2.0 K.' Those are polycrystals measured only to 2.0 K, above the bracketing Tc values (1.7 and 0.65 K), so the zero is very likely a measurement-floor null and not a contradiction. The same source probably explains the table's zero labels at x = 0.10 and x = 0.20, the bracketing compositions themselves.

Search for contrary reports measuring x near 0.15 below 2 K: FastTrack search_papers (two queries), alphaXiv discover_papers, an arXiv listing search (three queries), FastTrack get_citations on the Fei DOI (top 25 citing works), and reading of arXiv 1708.06537, 1212.5330, 1801.00050 and 1504.05295. None measured x = 0.15. Kiswandhi 2013 covered x = 0, 0.02, 0.03 and 0.05 under pressure; 1708.06537 covered x of 0.04-0.05; 1801.00050 covered x = 0.05. Takubo 2018 PRB covered 0 <= x <= 0.12 (abstract). Fu et al. measured x = 0.05, 0.1, 0.25 and 0.5: x = 0.1 has Tc about 2 K and x = 0.25 'does not appear at temperature above 0.3 K'. That is consistent with Fei's falling dome (about 0.4 K by interpolation at x = 0.25, a small difference within composition uncertainty) and says nothing against x = 0.15.

Not checked: Pyon, Kudo, Nohara, Physica C 494, 80 (2013), 10.1016/j.physc.2013.04.055. It is paywalled, OpenAlex and FastTrack give no abstract, and it is not on arXiv. Fei cites it as consistent for x = 0.1 (Tc about 1.7 K). Whether it measured x = 0.15 below 1 K is unknown.

sceptic.phase_or_sample: Bulk millimetre-sized single crystals grown from Te self-flux. CdI2-type 1T (P-3m1) phase stated to be pure by powder XRD (fit shown for x = 0.4). No structural or CDW transition in R(T) for x = 0.1-0.4 (Fig. 2c). Compositions are nominal flux-loading values; EDS is qualitative.
sceptic.page_table_or_figure: arXiv:1711.10909v1 (open-access copy of the DOI): superconductivity paragraph, PDF p. 9; Fig. 5a (R vs T for x = 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, falling to zero) and Fig. 5c (phase diagram), PDF p. 21; phase purity: text on PDF p. 6 and Fig. 2, PDF p. 18; Methods 'Crystal growth'.
sceptic.quote: For sample with x = 0.1, the superconducting transition temperature (Tc) is around 1.7 K, which is consistent with the previous report36. For sample with x = 0.2, the Tc decreases apparently to 0.65 K.
sceptic.tc_criterion: Estimate, not a measurement: linear interpolation at x = 0.15 between the resistive Tc values of the bracketing samples (1.7 K at x = 0.1, 0.65 K at x = 0.2). The authors' guide line in Fig. 5c passes about 1.1 K at x = 0.15 (read by eye). The paper does not define its Tc criterion. In Fig. 5a the 1.7 K label sits near mid-transition for x = 0.1 (zero resistance at about 1.4 K), and the 0.65 K label sits near zero resistance for x = 0.2.
sceptic.measurement_method: Electrical resistance versus temperature in a dilution refrigerator (to about 47 mK); upper critical field from R(T) in applied field (Fig. 5b). No magnetisation or specific-heat evidence for x >= 0.1.
sceptic.synthesis_conditions: Te self-flux: Ir powder, Pt sponge and Te shot in atomic ratio 0.18(1-x):0.18x:0.82 in an alumina crucible, vacuum-sealed; 950 C for 10 h, 1160 C for 24 h, slow cooling to 880 C over a week; flux removed by centrifugation.
sceptic.evidence_note: Fei et al. measured the 1T Ir1-xPtxTe2 single-crystal series down to 47 mK. x = 0.1 (1.7 K), x = 0.2 (0.65 K) and x = 0.3 (0.15 K) superconduct with zero resistance; x = 0.4 does not. The row, x = 0.15, sits 1.67 at.% Pt from each of the x = 0.1 and x = 0.2 samples, so it is bracketed within the 2 at.% limit by superconducting members of one single-phase series. The SuperCon zero matches Pyon et al. 2012, whose polycrystals were measured only down to 2.0 K. Fu et al. (arXiv:1712.02500) independently find x = 0.1 Te-flux crystals superconducting at about 2 K with EDX compositions matching nominal. Residual limits: compositions are nominal; the evidence is resistive only (zero resistance, no Meissner or specific-heat data at x >= 0.1); the published Adv. Mater. full text and Pyon et al. 2013 (Physica C) were not read. Tc at x = 0.15 is an interpolated estimate. Side note for whoever audits the neighbouring rows: the table's zero labels at Ir:0.300;Pt:0.033;Te:0.667 (x = 0.10) and Ir:0.267;Pt:0.067;Te:0.667 (x = 0.20) appear to come from the same 2.0 K-limited polycrystal null, while Fei reports both compositions superconducting.
sceptic.verifier_reason: I re-read the source myself (arXiv:1711.10909v1, the open-access copy linked to DOI 10.1002/adma.201801556, which Crossref confirms) and found the deciding statements and figures as both readers reported. Bulk single crystals of Ir1-xPtxTe2 at nominal x = 0.1 and x = 0.2, at ambient pressure, superconduct with zero resistance at 1.7 K and 0.65 K. Each sits 1.67 at.% Pt (1.70 and 1.63 at.% Ir) from the row Ir0.85Pt0.15Te2, inside the 2 at.% BRACKETED limit, in a series the authors describe as pure 1T phase with no low-temperature structural transition. I tried to refute this in four ways. (1) Impurity origin: no candidate impurity (Te, IrTe2, PtTe2, Ir metal, Pt-poor inclusions) can give the observed Tc values, and Tc and Hc2 fall smoothly with x as expected for the doped phase. (2) Composition: the labels are nominal, but an independent Te-flux study found EDX equal to nominal, and the row lies between two superconducting members either way. (3) Contrary measurements: the only null at this composition (Pyon et al. 2012) stops at 2.0 K, above both bracketing Tc values, and is very likely where the table's zero came from. No study measuring x = 0.15 below 2 K was found. (4) Revision in the published version: the published abstract still states superconductivity up to the Dirac-point composition (x = 0.3 in the preprint). The remaining limits are resistive-only evidence, nominal compositions, and the unread published full text and Pyon 2013. These are recorded caveats, not reasons of substance against the label correction. Apply, with Tc recorded as an interpolated estimate (about 1.2 K) and not as a measured value.

Sample form: the paper describes mm-sized bulk single crystals and gives no device or thin-flake fabrication for transport; the normal-state resistance of about 1.4 milliohm in Fig. 5a fits a bulk crystal rather than an exfoliated flake (my inference, not a statement in the paper). Caveats for the sceptic: (1) x is nominal (melt ratio), with only qualitative EDS; (2) I read the arXiv v1 preprint, not the published Wiley version, which has a different title and more authors, so the wording or numbers there could differ; (3) Tc criterion is not defined in the text; (4) the paper says the x = 0.1 Tc is 'consistent with the previous report' (ref. 36, Pyon, Kudo and Nohara, Physica C 494, 80 (2013)), which I could not open. A Tc of 1.7 K lies below the usual 1.8-2 K lower limit of many standard cryostats, which may explain why other measurements recorded this composition as non-superconducting; I did not verify that.

Also Pyon, Kudo, Nohara, Physica C 494, 80-84 (2013), doi 10.1016/j.physc.2013.04.055 (Pt-doped IrTe2 single crystals; cited as consistent for x = 0.1; check its x-T phase diagram and lowest measured temperature, since it may be the source of the zero-Tc SuperCon entries).

refutation_attempts: Re-read the source myself: downloaded arxiv.org/pdf/1711.10909 (v1, 21 pages), read the full text with pdftotext and viewed Fig. 2 (p. 18) and Fig. 5 (p. 21) as rendered images. The deciding sentence is on p. 9 (transport paragraph); p. 6 repeats it for Fig. 2c; Fig. 5a labels the x = 0.1 curve 'Tc = 1.7K' and shows the resistance falling to zero.

Composition arithmetic: Ir0.9Pt0.1Te2 has 3 atoms per formula unit: Ir 0.9/3 = 0.30000, Pt 0.1/3 = 0.03333, Te 2/3 = 0.66667. Row Ir 0.300, Pt 0.033, Te 0.667. Differences 0.00000, 0.00033, 0.00033 (at most 0.033 at.%), inside the 0.0015 limit. Checked that x is the Pt fraction: the Methods and one text line write 'IrxPt1-xTe2' (a typo), but the charge ratio Ir:Pt:Te = 0.18(1-x):0.18x:0.82, the Fig. 4 caption 'Ir0.8Pt0.2Te2' for x = 0.2, the Fig. 5c axis 'Pt doping x' and the loss of SC at high x all fix x as the Pt fraction.

Nominal versus measured composition: x is the nominal Pt fraction of the flux charge. EDS (Fig. 2b inset) only shows the Pt/Ir peak ratio rising with x; no measured x is given. This is a caveat, not a refutation: the table's own zero for this row most likely comes from Pyon et al. 2012, which also uses nominal compositions, and Fei's Tc at x = 0.1 fits smoothly between the table's neighbours x = 0.08 (2.38 K) and x = 0.12 (1.92 K).

Bulk or film: the samples are millimetre-sized hexagonal single crystals from Te self-flux (inset Fig. 2a). The paper describes no exfoliation into devices for transport. The normal-state resistance of about 1.4 milliohm in Fig. 5a fits a bulk crystal; a thin exfoliated flake of a metal with residual resistivity of tens of microohm-cm would show ohms, not milliohms (my estimate). Verdict: bulk.
Pressure: no applied pressure is mentioned anywhere; resistance was measured in a dilution refrigerator. Ambient.

Phase purity and whether SC belongs to the phase: powder XRD fitted with P-3m1 and called pure 1T phase (pattern shown for x = 0.4 only). Cooling and warming R(T) curves for x = 0.1 to 0.4 coincide with no jump (Fig. 2c), so no CDW/monoclinic transition. Plausible impurities do not superconduct near 1.7 K at ambient pressure (elemental Te no; Pt no; Ir only near 0.1 K; bulk IrTe2 no). The transition is a single sharp step to zero resistance. Evidence is resistive only (no susceptibility or specific heat for x = 0.1), but the rule asks for a bulk sample, not a thermodynamic probe, and the Tc fits the specific-heat-confirmed bulk dome of Pyon et al. 2012 continued to higher x.

Tc reading: from Fig. 5a (log temperature axis) I read the last normal-state point near 2.3 K, a point at about 1.15 of 1.4 milliohm near 1.8 K and the first zero point near 1.4 K, so the labelled 1.7 K sits near the midpoint of the drop. The Bc2(T) fit in Fig. 5b reaches zero field near 1700 mK. Reader A (midpoint) is closer to my reading than reader B (onset); this does not change the verdict.

Preprint versus published version: the published Adv. Mater. 30, 1801556 (2018) has a new title and 19 authors (v1 has 14). I could not read it: Wiley Scholar Gateway refused (free allowance used up until 1 Dec 2026). Its abstract (OpenAlex get_work) still says superconductivity is observed and persists when the Fermi level aligns with the Dirac points, which matches the preprint. OpenAlex lists the arXiv PDF as the open-access copy of this DOI.

DOI check: FastTrack verify_reference confirms 10.1002/adma.201801556 is registered with Crossref (Advanced Materials 30(35) 1801556, 2018, Fei et al.; no retraction flagged). OpenAlex get_work W2772494435 links it to arxiv.org/pdf/1711.10909.

Source of the table's zero: opened Pyon, Kudo, Nohara, JPSJ 81, 053701 (2012), arXiv:1204.1421. Polycrystalline Ir1-xPtxTe2, 0 <= x <= 0.25: 'No trace of superconductivity was observed for x >= 0.10 down to 2.0 K.' Fig. 1(b) caption: bars and arrows mark the absence of bulk SC above 2.0 K. That null stops at 2.0 K, above the 1.7 K Tc, so it does not contradict Fei. In Fei's data the x = 0.1 resistance at about 1.8 K is still about 80% of its normal value, so a 2.0 K floor would miss the transition.

Single-crystal corroboration: opened Takubo et al., PRB 97, 205142 (2018), arXiv:1805.05547. Its text says the SC dome lies in 0.04 <= x <= 0.12, and its Fig. 1(b) draws the SC region from Pyon, Kudo, Nohara, Physica C 494, 80 (2013) (single crystals; Tc scaled x10) reaching x of about 0.12 to 0.14, with Tc of roughly 2 K around x = 0.10 (my figure reading). This is a secondary depiction, used only to check for contradiction: it supports SC near x = 0.1 in single crystals and agrees with Fei's statement that x = 0.1 is 'consistent with the previous report'. Pyon et al. 2013 itself is paywalled and was not read.

reader_a.evidence_note: The 1977 abstract says the metallic lanthanum pnictide phases all superconduct below 1 K, that the anti-Th3P4-type compounds were studied in more detail, that Tc rises sharply in La4Bi3-xPbx as the electron count falls, and that Y on the La site lowers Tc. It does not name La4Sb2Sn or any Sn-substituted antimonide, and gives no Tc for it. The 1976 OSTI abstract says only that the La anti-Th3P4 compounds superconduct below 1 K and that cation and anion substitutions were studied. Neither abstract states a Tc or a null for this composition. It is not clear from the abstract whether 'all the metallic phases' covers the ternary substituted compounds such as La4Sb2Sn.
reader_a.reason_if_not: The primary paper (Hulliger and Ott 1977, Elsevier, closed access) and the 1976 AIP conference paper (OSTI holds no full text) could not be opened here. The abstracts I read do not state the composition La4Sb2Sn with a Tc, or a measurement down to a stated temperature without superconductivity. No open-access or arXiv copy, and no later primary paper giving a Tc for La4Sb2Sn or a La4Sb3-xSnx series, was found. Route STATED and route BRACKETED are both unmet, and there is no basis for verified_null.
reader_a.leads_for_library: F. Hulliger and H. R. Ott, 'Superconductivity of lanthanum pnictides', J. Less-Common Met. 55 (1977) 103-113, doi:10.1016/0022-5088(77)90266-1: look in the table of anti-Th3P4-type compounds and substituted variants (La4Sb3, La4Sb2Sn, La4Sb2Pb, La4Bi3-xPbx, La3YSb3) for the Tc or the 'not superconducting above T' entry for La4Sb2Sn, and note the lowest temperature reached (the measurements went below 1 K). Also F. Hulliger and H. R. Ott, 'Superconductivity in compounds with anti-Th3P4 structure', AIP Conf. Proc. 34 (1976), OSTI 7230802. Secondary: F. Hulliger, 'Rare earth pnictides', Handbook on the Physics and Chemistry of Rare Earths vol. 4, ch. 33 (1979), doi:10.1016/S0168-1273(79)04006-X, may tabulate the same Tc values. COD 1538301 (La4Sb2Sn structure from the 1977 paper).

The Khan and Raub 1975 gold-alloy review (secondary) says the gold-rich solid solutions studied were not superconducting. I found no paper that reports Au3Hg or a bracketing Au-Hg series as superconducting at ambient pressure. The full Luo-Andres text could be checked for an Au-Hg entry, but nothing points to one.

reader_a.evidence_note: No primary paper reporting a measurement on Nb80Ti19Fe1 (or on Ti80Nb19Fe1), or on a Nb-Ti-Fe series bracketing it, was found or opened in this session. arXiv:2512.18821 (Kushwaha et al., 2025) was read in full. It reports bulk arc-melted bcc Nb0.85Ti0.15 (also Nb0.85Zr0.15 and Nb0.85Hf0.15), with Tc 9.65(2) K from magnetization and 9.68(2) K from zero resistivity, at ambient pressure. It has no Fe-containing sample and no sample at Nb80Ti20, so it does not decide this row. The only Ti-Nb-Fe superconductivity paper the searches found is Prokoshkin and Puzei, 1970 (OpenAlex W236250958; ADS 1970ZhPmR..11..493P; JETP Lett. 11, 336). It is closed access, it was not opened, and its alloy composition is unknown. The other leads are binary Nb-Ti work with no Fe (Shapira and Neuringer 1965: Nb-37 and Nb-56 at.% Ti; Sukharevskii, Shchetkin and Fal'ko, JETP 33, 152, 1971; Shchetkin and Kharchenko, JETP 1973) or industrial ppm-level Fe in Nb-47wt%Ti (Smathers 1996). None states this composition. From physics alone, a Nb-rich bcc Nb-Ti alloy with 1 at.% Fe would be expected to superconduct near 9 K. That expectation is not evidence under the owner's rule.

screen.reason: Ti2CdC is an H-phase (MAX) carbide first made by Jeitschko, Nowotny and Benesovsky in 1964. Toth, Jeitschko and Yen 1966 tested a representative set of isotypic H-phases for superconductivity and report no transitions in the indexed abstract (the stated lower temperature limit reads garbled, '11 K' or '1.1 K'). That paper is a plausible source of the null, but the abstract does not list which phases were sampled. Later MAX-phase superconductivity reports (Nb2SnC, Nb2InC, Ti2InC, Ti2InN, Nb2GeC) do not include Ti2CdC, and the Ti2CdC papers I found are DFT studies of elastic and electronic properties. I found no report that Ti2CdC superconducts.

Bulk and ambient pressure: polycrystalline powders from hydrothermal synthesis (155 C, 7 days). PXRD 'revealed single phase samples'. Lattice parameters vary linearly with x for 0 <= x < 1 (homogeneous substitution). SQUID and ac-susceptibility measurements with no applied pressure. Not a film or nanostructure.

Phase attribution: the 35-38 K transition is not an impurity's. Hydrothermal FeSe is non-superconducting or about 8 K, and FeS is about 5 K or below. Tc in this series moves continuously with x from 43 K (x = 1) to zero at x = 0, so the transition belongs to the intercalated main phase. My pixel reading of Fig. 4 for x = 0.92: ZFC 4 pi chi leaves zero at about 35-37 K, is about -0.13 near 31 K, and reaches about -0.72 at 2 K (3 mT, not demagnetization corrected). That is a large shielding fraction, not a trace. FC is only slightly negative; the paper explains this by the coexisting ferromagnetism of the hydroxide layer, which is also seen in the parent selenide.

Ferromagnetism as an alternative explanation: the Fig. 4 diamagnetism is negative, and the pure sulphide (x = 0, same ferromagnetic layer) stays positive throughout. So the negative signal is not magnetic ordering. The Fig. 5 initial curve for x = 0.92 dips to about -0.5 muB per Fe at low field, unlike x = 0.

Where the table's zero most likely came from: Lu et al. (arXiv:1501.01157 = PRB 90, 214520), which I downloaded and read, list an EDX x = 0.08 sample (S0.08Se0.92, this row) among their 11 samples. Their Fig. 2 susceptibility panels and their Fig. 5 phase diagram (both viewed) show no curve and no Tc point for x = 0.08. The other table rows in this system (S 0.032 to 0.154 superconducting, S 0.180 not) match Lu et al.'s x = 0.16 to 0.90 points. A SuperCon record for the x = 0.08 sample with no Tc would most likely have become the table's zero. Lu et al. do not report x = 0.08 as non-superconducting; they state Tc 'vanishes at x = 0.90' and is 'suppressed from 40 K to zero as S content increases from 0 to 0.90'.

Independent bracket (supporting, not needed for the stated route): in Lu et al. Fig. 5, x = 0 (S 0, Se 0.200, Tc about 41 K) and x = 0.16 (S 0.032, Se 0.168, Tc about 38.5 K; the text gives 69% ZFC shielding at 5 K, 'bulk superconductivity at 37 K') are each 1.6 at.% from the row on S and Se and 0 on the other elements. Both are superconducting. Lu et al.'s XRD shows a broad peak attributed to nanoscale FeS (an impurity, not superconducting at these temperatures). Within Pachmayr's own series, x = 0.88 (S 0.024, 0.8 at.% away, Tc about 35-37 K) and x = 0.97 (S 0.006, 1.0 at.% away, Tc about 38 K) are also superconducting.

sceptic.verifier_reason: I re-read the paper both readers cite (arXiv:1412.6475, the preprint of Chem. Commun. 51, 4689; DOI checked with Crossref) and found nothing of substance to refute them. Its x = 0.92 sample, [(Li0.8Fe0.2)OH]Fe(S0.08Se0.92), matches the row exactly in atomic fractions. It is a bulk hydrothermal powder, single phase by PXRD, measured at ambient pressure. Fig. 4 shows strong zero-field-cooled diamagnetism from about 36 K to 4 pi chi of about -0.72 at 2 K, and Fig. 5 shows a superconducting initial magnetization curve at 1.8 K. Tc changes continuously with Se content, which ties the superconductivity to the main phase and not to an FeSe or FeS impurity. The coexisting ferromagnetism cannot produce a negative signal: the ferromagnetic pure sulphide stays positive. No paper I found reports this composition as non-superconducting. The likely origin of the zero is Lu et al.'s EDX x = 0.08 sample, which they list but never show a result for. Their own phase diagram puts superconducting points at 1.6 at.% on either side (x = 0, about 41 K; x = 0.16, about 38.5 K), and they state that superconductivity vanishes only at x = 0.90. Remaining caveats: Tc is read from a figure (about 36 K by dc onset, about 38 K from the ac-susceptibility inset), and the published RSC version and its ESI were not opened; I read the arXiv preprint of the same paper.

This is exactly the row (0.00 at.% difference) and independently supports superconductivity at this composition; it was read only by the sceptic, so it is recorded as support, not as the two-reader evidence.

Contrary report examined: Sharma et al., PRB 81, 174512 (2010), arXiv:0902.2728 read in full; DOI Crossref-verified. Polycrystalline BaFe2-xRuxAs2 by solid-state reaction, nominal x = 0.50 = exactly the row (nominal only). My 400-dpi zoom of the R(T) figure (PDF p.15, the panel captioned Fig. 2) shows the x = 0.5 curve continuing down to about 4-5 K with only the SDW anomaly and no superconducting drop; Reader A's statement that this curve stops at about 25 K is wrong, Reader B's reading (down to about 4-5 K) is right. Its phase diagram (PDF p.16) plots Tc = 0 at x = 0.5 and TSDW about 137 K; Mossbauer at 5 K shows magnetic splitting. The text gives no lowest temperature for x = 0.5 and reports superconductivity only for nominal x = 0.75-1.125.

Weighing the contrary report: the same paper places TSDW at about 145 K (nominal x = 0.25), 137 K (0.5), 128 K (0.625) and 97 K coexisting with zero-resistance SC at 0.75, while the three single-crystal series with measured composition put the structural/magnetic transition near 30 K (Thaler x_WDS 0.24) or 50 K (Rullier-Albenque x = 0.26) at the row's composition and suppress it fully by about 0.29-0.35 per TM. The polycrystal series is therefore shifted by roughly a factor of two in nominal Ru relative to every measured-composition series; its Ru content was refined only for x = 0.875, and it contains Ru/Fe and Ba arsenide impurity peaks. The paper does not let one tell whether the cause is inhomogeneity or lower Ru in the 122 phase, but its nominal x = 0.5 sample behaved magnetically like a much lower-Ru sample. It is the likely origin of the table's zero, not evidence that homogeneous Ba(Fe0.75Ru0.25)2As2 fails to superconduct.

Later corrections: none found. Crossref records for Thaler and Sharma show no retraction flag (which is not proof of none). Thaler is cited about 100 times; the later literature (Eom 2012, Xing 2012, Sharma et al. 2015 Acta Cryst. B, arXiv:1312.7055, which cites Thaler and Rullier-Albenque as 'the known phase diagram') treats x ~ 0.25 per TM as superconducting.

Second possible contrary lead: Reddy et al., J. Phys.: Condens. Matter 26, 356002 (2014), DOI 10.1088/0953-8984/26/35/356002: abstract only (OpenAlex record); Mossbauer on powdered single crystals of BaFe2-xRuxAs2 x = 0-0.5 shows magnetic hyperfine fields at 5 K for x = 0.5. The abstract says nothing about superconductivity. Magnetic order coexists with superconductivity at this composition in the single-crystal studies (Thaler Fig. 8, Rullier-Albenque Fig. 3), so the abstract is not a null. Full text not obtained (Firecrawl scrape of the IOP PDF returned an IOP error page).
