refutation_attempts: Composition arithmetic: the row is Ba(Fe1-xCox)2As2 with x = 0.014*5/2 = 0.035 (Co 2(0.035)/5 = 0.0140, Fe 2(0.965)/5 = 0.3860, Ba 0.200, As 0.400). Ni et al. x = 0.038: Co 0.0152, Fe 0.3848, differences 0.12 at.% on Co and Fe (inside 0.15 at.%, as both readers said). Chu et al. x = 0.035: exact match. Hodovanets et al. x = 0.034: Co 0.0136, Fe 0.3864, differences 0.04 at.%. Hardy et al. x = 3.5 % = 0.035: exact match. Bernhard et al. x = 0.03 and 0.04: Co 0.0120 and 0.0160, 0.20 at.% away (outside the window).

Re-read Ni et al. (arXiv:0811.1767v1, preprint of PRB 78, 214515) myself: Results text p.5 and Summary p.10 state superconductivity for x >= 0.038; Fig. 4 inset (p.17) shows the x = 0.038 resistance reaching zero near 10 K; Fig. 6 (p.19) shows ZFC M/H about -1.1 (1/4pi) at 2 K for x = 0.038 (near-full shielding), FC small. Bulk self-flux single crystals, no impurity phase in powder XRD, ambient pressure. The readers' reading of this paper is correct.

Re-read Chu et al. (arXiv:0811.2463v1, preprint of PRB 79, 014506) myself: Fig. 1 (p.2) x = 0.035 curve (offset 0.8) falls from about 1.65 to about 0.80, i.e. to its zero baseline, only at the lowest temperatures (about 2 K); midpoint about 5 K. The text says 'For samples with x > 0.035 superconductivity is evident from a sharp drop to zero in the resistivity', so the authors' own wording does not include x = 0.035 in the sharp-transition group, although Fig. 6 and the abstract put x = 0.035 inside the dome. Their x = 0.025 is not superconducting.

Bulk vs film, pressure, phase: all papers considered are bulk single crystals at ambient pressure; no foreign superconducting phase is involved. Superconductivity at x ~ 0.035-0.04 coexists with the orthorhombic/SDW state; Ni et al. and Bernhard et al. note possible phase separation within the same compound and that x = 0.04 is a borderline case for bulk superconductivity (Bernhard: 'The sample at x = 0.04 with Tc = 6 K is a borderline case where our muSR data do not provide a solid proof that superconductivity is a bulk phenomenon').

Searched for further samples at x ~ 0.034-0.036 (arXiv full-text grep of 20 Ba(Fe1-xCox)2As2 papers). Found Hodovanets et al., Phil. Mag. 93, 661 (2013), arXiv:1206.2891 (Canfield group, WDS x): 'SC appears for x=0.034 of Co in accordance with resistance and magnetization measurements'; Fig. 2(b) shows x = 0.034 resistance falling to zero near 5-7 K and Fig. 6 plots Tc about 7-8 K; samples with x < 0.034 show no SC. This supports the readers.

Searched for contrary reports and found one at the exact composition: Hardy et al., EPL 91, 47008 (2010), arXiv:1007.2218v1 (Karlsruhe crystals, Co by EDX). Fig. 1(a) (p.2) shows a single crystal with x = 3.5 (%, i.e. x = 0.035; table gamma_n = 13.2, B3 = 0.45, Theta_D = 163) among the samples the text calls 'non-superconducting underdoped (x < 0.04)'; its C/T vs T^2 is a straight Debye line with no anomaly from 0.4 K to about 6 K. Superconducting crystals in that paper start at x = 0.04 (Tc = 5.8 K). A crystal of the row's composition was therefore measured as non-superconducting (bulk probe) down to 0.4 K.

Bernhard et al., PRB 86, 184509 (2012), arXiv:1206.7085 (crystals from the same Karlsruhe growth source, T. Wolf; EDX x): 'In the non-superconducting samples at 0 < x < 0.04 ...'; their x = 0.02 and 0.03 are non-superconducting and x = 0.04 has Tc = 6 K. Their methods paragraph cites Hardy et al. as indicating bulk SC for 0.035 <= x <= 0.13, which conflicts with Hardy's own Fig. 1(a); I take Hardy's figure as the primary statement.

Where the table's zero probably comes from: Hardy et al.'s x = 3.5 % non-superconducting crystal matches the row exactly (Co 0.014, Fe 0.386). I could not see the SuperCon record itself, so this attribution is a likely source, not a confirmed one.
Later corrections: none found for Ni et al., Chu et al. or Hardy et al. (Crossref shows no retraction flags; arXiv lists only v1 for each). Published journal versions were not opened.

sceptic.evidence_note: Not applied, so no evidence row. For the record, the supporting primary sources I re-read are: Ni et al. PRB 78, 214515 (10.1103/PhysRevB.78.214515), x = 0.038, resistive offset about 10 K, ZFC near-full shielding, Fig. 4 inset and Fig. 6; Chu et al. PRB 79, 014506 (10.1103/PhysRevB.79.014506), x = 0.035, resistive midpoint about 5 K, Figs. 1 and 6; Hodovanets et al. Phil. Mag. 93, 661 (10.1080/14786435.2012.729866), x = 0.034, Tc about 7-8 K, Figs. 2(b) and 6. All DOIs verified with Crossref via FastTrack verify_reference.
sceptic.verifier_reason: Both readers read Ni et al. correctly: an x = 0.038 bulk single crystal, 0.12 at.% from the row, superconducts at ambient pressure (resistance to zero near 10 K, near-full ZFC shielding). I also found a closer Canfield-group sample (Hodovanets et al., x = 0.034, 0.04 at.% away) that superconducts near 7-8 K, and Chu et al.'s x = 0.035 crystal reaches zero resistance only near 2 K. The label is still not safe to change. Hardy et al., EPL 91, 47008 (2010), report a Ba(Fe0.965Co0.035)2As2 single crystal, exactly the row composition, as non-superconducting: its specific heat shows no anomaly down to 0.4 K, and superconductivity in that series starts at x = 0.04. Bernhard et al. (same crystal source) likewise find no superconductivity for 0 < x < 0.04. The row sits on the steep underdoped edge of the dome, where the onset lies between x of about 0.025 and 0.04 depending on the laboratory and its Co analysis (EDX, WDS, EMPA), and where Tc changes from 0 to about 10 K within 0.005 in x. So the same nominal composition is reported both superconducting (Chu; Hodovanets and Ni within the window) and non-superconducting down to 0.4 K (Hardy), and Hardy's entry is the likely origin of the table's zero. A primary report that measured this composition and found no superconductivity is a reason of substance to doubt the correction, so under the owner's rule and 'when in doubt, do_not_apply' the zero label stays. A person could revisit this if the project adopts a rule for compositions with conflicting primary reports, for example by using the Co scale of one reference laboratory.

reader_a.evidence_note: Fang et al. (Wen group, IOP Beijing) measured a series of Ba(Fe1-xCox)2As2 single crystals with x = 0, 0.02, 0.04, 0.05, 0.06, 0.07, 0.08, 0.10, 0.12, 0.15, 0.30 (Fig. 1(a)); Fig. 1(b) also plots 0.18 and 0.20. The x = 0.15 crystal is superconducting by three signs in the paper: resistivity reaching zero (Fig. 1(a)), a full diamagnetic transition in the inset that the caption says shows superconducting samples, and a plotted Tc of about 11.5 K in the phase diagram. The row (x = 0.1525) is within 0.10 at.% of x = 0.15 on Co and Fe. Points for the sceptic: (1) x is nominal; the paper says only that EDX found the actual Co 'close to the nominal values'. (2) Ning et al., PRL 104, 037001 (2010) (DOI 10.1103/PhysRevLett.104.037001; arXiv:0907.3875, opened), used crystals from the same group (their ref. [10] is Fang et al.) with EDX-measured x. Their Fig. 1 plots the EDX x = 0.14 sample at Tc of about 0, and their text says x = 0.14 was measured at 4.2 K (> Tc). Their introduction says the system becomes non-superconducting above x ~ 0.15, citing Ni et al. and Fang et al.; that is a general statement, not a measurement at x = 0.15. Their next sample is x = 0.26, which is non-superconducting. (3) Chu et al., PRB 79, 014506 (2009) (arXiv:0811.2463, opened): superconductivity for 0.025 < x < 0.18 with microprobe-measured x. Their x = 0.140 sample lies inside that range, and for x = 0.184 Tc is below their 1.8 K base. So Chu agrees that x ~ 0.15 sits inside the superconducting dome. Note that Chu's 'x = 0.061' is the optimal doping on the Fe site (Tc 24 K), which is not the same quantity as the row's Co atomic fraction 0.061. Inside Fang Fig. 1(b), the inset magnetization transitions for low x (e.g. 0.05 near 4 K) do not match the main-panel Tc values (0.05 near 11 K), so the figure's Tc values carry some uncertainty; the 0.15 sample is still shown superconducting in all three.

refutation_attempts: Re-read the cited source myself: arXiv:0903.2418v3 (Fang et al., same authors and title as PRB 80, 140508(R)), text and Fig. 1 at 250 and 600 dpi. Confirmed what the readers report: the nominal x = 0.15 crystal's resistivity (purple pentagons, Fig. 1(a)) falls from about 10-11 K to zero near 7-8 K; the Fig. 1(b) inset (caption: 'diamagnetic signal measured in superconducting samples') has a 0.15 curve with a full normalized diamagnetic transition at about 7-8 K; the phase diagram puts x = 0.15 at about 11-12 K. The text states that superconductivity 'vanishes at a doping level of 18-20%'. The x values are nominal; the paper says only that EDX found the actual Co 'close to the nominal values' and gives no measured x per crystal.

At.% arithmetic: Fang nominal Ba(Fe0.85Co0.15)2As2 = Ba 0.2000, Fe 0.3400, Co 0.0600, As 0.4000; differences from the row are 0.10 at.% on Fe and Co, within 0.15 at.%. The arithmetic holds for the nominal formula. The row's Co 0.061 corresponds to x = 0.1525 (range 0.15125-0.15375 given rounding), which matches an EDX-measured x = 0.153 exactly (Co 0.0612, Fe 0.3388).
Bulk and pressure: Fang's samples are FeAs-flux single crystals measured in a PPMS with no applied pressure. No issue there.

Contrary reports for the same composition: Hardy et al., EPL 91, 47008 (2010), arXiv:1007.2218 (opened, full text and Fig. 1). These are Karlsruhe self-flux single crystals with composition 'determined by energy dispersive x-ray spectroscopy and complemented by 4-circle diffractometry'. Fig. 1(b) shows a crystal with x = 15.3% (EDX). Its specific heat C/T is linear in T^2 down to 0.4 K, with no transition. The text calls the overdoped crystals with x >= 0.14 'non-superconducting' and uses the x = 0.153 crystal as the lattice reference for the superconducting overdoped samples. In their series Tc is 11.1 K at x = 0.112 and 5.1 K at x = 0.12, and they place the collapse of superconductivity around x = 0.13. This is a bulk, thermodynamic, ambient-pressure null at exactly the row's composition (Co 0.0612 vs 0.061). It is the most likely source of the table's zero reports.

Composition-scale problem: Hardy et al. also write that 'the effective Co amount in the sample represents only 75 % of the nominal flux Co content', as other groups found. Fang's x = 0.15 is nominal, and its EDX check is reported only as 'close to nominal', so Fang's actual Co content is not pinned to within 0.15 at.%. Ning et al., PRL 104, 037001 (2010), arXiv:0907.3875 (opened), used crystals from the Fang/Wen group (their ref. [10]) with EDX-measured x. Their Fig. 1 plots the EDX x = 0.14 crystal at Tc of about 0, inside the 'overdoped non-superconducting' side of the diagram. That fits a Wen-group nominal-to-actual offset and weakens Fang's nominal 0.15 as evidence for an actual x = 0.1525.

Supporting reports also checked: Kim et al., PRB 86, 014513 (2012), arXiv:1206.5354 (opened). Annealed ORNL-grown crystals 'x = 0.15' with Tc = 11.7 K from bulk specific heat. Their composition method is not stated in what I read. Their note 21 states that 'lack of precise correspondence between nominal composition and actual measured physical properties are common in the 122 iron superconductors'. Mun et al. (Canfield group), arXiv:0906.1548 (opened): with WDS-measured x, Co-doped superconductivity spans x ~ 0.035 to ~ 0.17, and the literature points in their Fig. 1(b) show about 8 K near x_WDS ~ 0.135 and Tc = 0 near x_WDS ~ 0.166. Chu et al., arXiv:0811.2463 (opened): superconductivity for 0.025 < x < 0.18 by microprobe; x = 0.140 is superconducting, and x = 0.184 has Tc below 1.8 K; no sample near 0.15.

Net: at x ~ 0.15 the groups disagree. Fang (nominal) and Kim/ORNL report superconductivity at 7-12 K. Hardy/Karlsruhe (EDX x = 0.153) reports no superconductivity down to 0.4 K. Canfield (WDS) and Chu (microprobe) put x ~ 0.15 near the overdoped edge without measuring it. Which result applies depends on whose composition scale is right, and the sample matching the row's measured composition is non-superconducting.

sceptic.evidence_note: Readers A and B read Fang et al. correctly: their nominal x = 0.15 crystal superconducts at about 7-12 K, and the nominal formula is within 0.10 at.% of the row. The refutation is not about their reading. It comes from a separate, primary, bulk measurement at the row's own measured composition, which found no superconductivity down to 0.4 K.
sceptic.verifier_reason: I do not apply this correction. I re-read Fang et al. (arXiv:0903.2418v3, DOI 10.1103/PhysRevB.80.140508, verified) and agree that its nominal Ba(Fe0.85Co0.15)2As2 crystal superconducts: resistivity reaches zero near 7-8 K and there is a full diamagnetic transition in Fig. 1. The nominal formula is within 0.10 at.% of the row. But Fang's x is nominal, and the overdoped edge of the Ba(Fe1-xCox)2As2 dome sits right at this composition, where Tc changes by several K per 0.01 in x and groups' composition scales differ. Hardy et al., EPL 91, 47008 (2010) (DOI 10.1209/0295-5075/91/47008, verified; full text read on arXiv:1007.2218) measured an EDX-determined x = 0.153 bulk single crystal. That is Co 0.0612 and Fe 0.3388, matching the row to 0.02 at.%. They found no superconducting transition in specific heat down to 0.4 K and explicitly call crystals with x >= 0.14 non-superconducting. They also note that effective Co is only about 75% of the nominal flux Co. Ning et al. (PRL 104, 037001), using crystals from Fang's own group, place an EDX x = 0.14 crystal at Tc of about 0. Against these, Kim et al. (PRB 86, 014513) report an ORNL 'x = 0.15' crystal at 11.7 K, and Canfield's WDS dome ends near x ~ 0.166. So the literature is in direct conflict at this composition. The only report with a measured composition equal to the row's is a bulk, ambient-pressure null to 0.4 K, which is a plausible origin of the table's zero labels. That is a reason of substance to doubt that this composition, as a bulk sample, superconducts, so the label 'not a superconductor' stays.

refutation_attempts: Source re-read: I opened https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/6215146 myself (LANL report LA-UR-84-3487, 12 pages of text: the author manuscript of J. Appl. Phys. 57, 3137 (1985), same title and the same four authors). I also read the published abstract of DOI 10.1063/1.335182 through OpenAlex get_work. It states the same Tc (1.1 K for C14) and the same C15 null (none above 70 mK). The published AIP full text is closed and I did not open it.

Deciding statements found: Abstract ('The C14 phase has been found to exhibit superconductivity with a superconducting transition temperature Tc of 1.1 K, while the C15 phase does not display superconductivity above 70 mK'); Introduction paragraph 1 ('the Cl4 phase of CeOs2 is a superconductor at 1.1 K'); Table I, row Tc: C14 1.1 K, C15 '--'.

Composition arithmetic: CeOs2 gives Ce = 1/3 = 0.33333 and Os = 2/3 = 0.66667. The row has Ce 0.333 and Os 0.667. |dCe| = 0.00033 (0.033 at.%) and |dOs| = 0.00033 (0.033 at.%), both under the 0.0015 (0.15 at.%) limit. The paper says the two polymorphs differ in structure 'without a change in composition', and both were cut from one master ingot.
Bulk or film: bulk. Measurements were made on 'unannealed and annealed pieces ... cut from the master ingot'. There is no film or nanostructure.

Pressure: the C15-to-C14 transformation 'can be accomplished at ambient pressure by annealing at temperatures between 500 and 950°C'. No applied pressure is mentioned for any measurement. Earlier high-pressure annealing routes (Cannon et al. 1973, their Ref. 2) were not used for these samples.

Phase attribution and impurities: the authors assign the 1.1 K transition to the C14 phase of CeOs2. Their own C15 pieces from the same ingot, measured to 70 mK, show no superconductivity, so the transition does not come from something common to the ingot. 1.1 K does not match elemental Os (about 0.66 K; this is a standard handbook value that I did not re-check in this session). Os is the only plausible elemental impurity, because Ce does not superconduct at ambient pressure. If an annealed piece were only partly transformed, the remainder would still be CeOs2 (C15) and not a different compound. Weak point: this paper gives no X-ray phase-purity data and does not define the Tc criterion; both are in its Ref. 4 (Torikachvili, Maple, Meisner, LT-17 proceedings 1984, p. 329), which I could not open.

Independent corroboration searched: Sugawara, Sato, Aoki et al., J. Phys. Soc. Jpn. 66, 174 (1997), DOI 10.1143/jpsj.66.174, and Czech. J. Phys. (1996), DOI 10.1007/bf02570272, abstracts read (FastTrack, SciSpace). A different group prepared both phases and writes 'This fact explains why only the C14 becomes superconductive.' That accepts, and does not dispute, the superconductivity of the C14 phase. Their own Tc value is not in the abstracts.
Later corrections or retractions: none found. The FastTrack record shows no retraction flag, and the paper's citing works found in searches do not dispute the C14 result.

Origin of the table's zeros: the zeros very probably come from the C15 (cubic, as-cast or quenched) form of CeOs2. That form is reported non-superconducting in this same paper (no transition above 70 mK). The C15 CeRu2-xOsx series is also studied by Hiebl et al., Physica B+C 130, 129 (1985), DOI 10.1016/0378-4363(85)90203-7. Its abstract, read via SciSpace, reports a complete cubic MgCu2-type solid solution at 1250 °C and Tc depressed at dTc/dx = -0.117 K/mol%. And by Wilhelm & Hillenbrand, Z. Naturforsch. A 26, (1971), DOI 10.1515/zna-1971-0126; the abstract mentions Ce(Ru1-xOsx)2 Tc data, and the full-text scrape failed. These are measured nulls for the cubic polymorph only. They do not touch the hexagonal C14 polymorph of the same composition, which is made at ambient pressure.

DOI check: FastTrack verify_reference on 10.1063/1.335182 returned 'registered with Crossref': J. Appl. Phys. 57(8), 3137-3139, 1985, Torikachvili, Yang, Maple, Meisner, which matches the OSTI manuscript's title and authors.
contrary_reports: Same paper (DOI 10.1063/1.335182): the cubic C15 polymorph of CeOs2 is not superconducting above 70 mK (0.07 K). This is a measured null for the same composition in a different crystal structure, not for the C14 phase that carries the superconductivity.

Hiebl et al., Physica B+C 130, 129 (1985), DOI 10.1016/0378-4363(85)90203-7 (abstract only): C15 CeRu2-xOsx solid solution, Tc falls with Os content. The abstract does not state a CeOs2 Tc or a lowest temperature, and it concerns the cubic phase only.

No report of a non-superconducting C14 (hexagonal) CeOs2 sample was found. Searches run: FastTrack search_papers 'CeOs2 Laves phase superconductivity C14 C15' and 'CeRu2-xOsx superconductivity pseudobinary Laves Ce(Ru,Os)2'; SciSpace search 'Is the Laves phase compound CeOs2 superconducting, and in which crystal structure (C14 or C15)?'; WebSearch 'CeOs2 superconductivity C14 hexagonal 1.1 K Torikachvili' and '"CeOs2" superconducting OR superconductivity Laves cerium osmium'. OpenAlex search_works (daily budget used up) and Consensus (usage exhausted) did not run.

sceptic.evidence_note: The exact composition CeOs2 is stated to superconduct at Tc = 1.1 K in its hexagonal C14 polymorph, a bulk piece made and measured at ambient pressure (route STATED). The same paper reports that the cubic C15 polymorph of the same composition shows no superconductivity down to 70 mK, so the label is polymorph-dependent. The table's 'not a superconductor' zeros very probably come from the C15 form. The paper gives no separate lowest temperature for the C14 sample, so lowest_measured_temperature_k is null; the 70 mK limit applies to the C15 sample. An independent group (Sugawara et al., JPSJ 66, 174 (1997)) prepared both polymorphs and states that only C14 becomes superconducting. The text read is the LANL author manuscript of the published paper; the published abstract states the same values.
sceptic.verifier_reason: I re-read the deciding source myself: the OSTI author manuscript (LA-UR-84-3487) of Torikachvili, Yang, Maple and Meisner, J. Appl. Phys. 57, 3137 (1985), plus the published abstract. The DOI is registered with Crossref and matches. Its abstract, introduction and Table I state Tc = 1.1 K for CeOs2 in the C14 structure, in bulk pieces of one master ingot annealed at ambient pressure. The composition matches the row to 0.033 at.% on both elements. I tried to refute this and could not. The superconductivity is assigned to the CeOs2 C14 phase, and the C15 pieces from the same ingot do not superconduct, which argues against an ingot-wide impurity. 1.1 K does not match elemental Os. No pressure, film or theory is involved. An independent later group accepts that C14 CeOs2 superconducts. The only contrary measurements I found are for the cubic C15 polymorph: this paper's own null above 70 mK, and the C15 CeRu2-xOsx series. They are the likely origin of the table's zeros, but they do not show that the composition fails to superconduct in bulk at ambient pressure. Two limits remain. The Tc criterion and the phase-purity data are only in the paper's LT-17 Ref. 4, which I could not open. And the label depends on polymorph: CeOs2 superconducts as C14 and not as C15. Neither limit is a reason of substance under the owner's rule, so the correction applies, and the polymorph should be recorded in the evidence.

reader_a.evidence_note: Nagao (2015), arXiv 1511.00219 = Novel Supercond. Mater. 1, 10.1515/nsm-2015-0007, Table I lists flux-grown Ce(O,F)BiS2 single crystals with analytical F/(F+O) y = 0.24 (Tc 3.0 K) and y = 0.26 (Tc 3.2 K), which bracket the row (y = 0.25) within 0.2 at.% on each side. Both are superconducting by magnetization; Fig. 13 shows zero resistance and diamagnetism for the y = 0.24 crystal. Points for the auditor and sceptic: (1) The paper calls itself a review ('This review focuses on the growth and characterization of R(O,F)BiS2 ...'), but it is the crystal grower's own data: it has its own Experimental section and Table I carries no outside citation. The y = 0.26 (x = 0.6) Ce crystal appears neither in Nagao et al. SSC 178, 33 (2014) (Ce x = 0.3, 0.7, 0.9 only) nor in the reprinted Miura et al. CGD Table II (x = 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9), so this paper is the only report I found for it. I count it as primary for Table I. If it is treated as secondary, the CGD crystals reprinted in its Table II (y = 0.24, Tc 3.0 K; y = 0.27, Tc 3.1 K) also bracket the row within 0.2 and 0.4 at.%, but I could not open CGD itself. (2) The Ce y values depend on a large overlap correction: the same group's SSC 2014 paper gave uncorrected y = 0.53, 0.65 and 0.66 for x = 0.3, 0.7 and 0.9, and the 2015 paper subtracts 0.37 from each. No error bars are given. (3) CONTRARY REPORT at the exact nominal composition: Xing et al., PRB 86, 214518 (2012) (arXiv 1208.5000), polycrystalline CeO1-xFxBiS2 made by solid-state reaction (>90% main phase, <10% Ce2O2S). Fig. 2(c) plots Tc = 0 for nominal x = 0.25 (= this row exactly). Fig. 2(b) shows no transition in resistivity down to about 2 K, and the text says 'superconductivity appears at about x = 0.33'. F content was checked only by EDX ('close to the nominal one'). The two series can be reconciled if the polycrystal's real F content is below its nominal value, but this paper does not establish that. On the face of the text, the bracketed route is met by analytically measured compositions; whether that outweighs the nominal-composition null is for the sceptic.

Its resistivity in Fig. 2(b) is flat at about 4 mOhm cm from 8 K down to the lowest point at 2 K, and Fig. 2(c) plots its Tc as 0; the text puts the onset of superconductivity at about x = 0.33.
